S.O. 837.—Whereas the use of Aadhaar number to establish identity enabling individuals to receive 
subsidies, benefits and services in a convenient and seamless manner, obviates the need for multiplicity of documents 
to establish identity, simplifies the processes and promotes transparency and efficiency; 


And whereas, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, Government of India, after 
consultation with the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI), had conveyed vide its letter No. 3(3)/2023- 
EG-II, dated the 50 May, 2025 to the Ministry of Finance, Department of Financial Services, Government of India 
(hereinafter referred to as the said Ministry) for the purposes prescribed under sub-rule (.) of rule 3 of the Aadhaar 
Authentication for Good Governance (Social Welfare, Innovation, Knowledge) Rules, 2020 (hereinafter referred to as 
the said rules) that the Institute of Banking Personnel Selection (IBPS) (hereinafter referred to as the said Agency) 
may be allowed to perform authentication and be permitted the use of Aadhaar number during authentication for 
establishing identity of Aadhaar number holder and notify the same under rule 5 of the said rules read with sub-clause 
(ii) of clause (b) of sub-section (4) of section 4 of the Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, 
Benefits and Services) Act, 20l6 (8 of 20I6) (hereinafter referred to as the said Act); 


And whereas, the Aadhaar authentication shall be performed for usage of digital platforms to ensure good 
governance (hereinafter referred to as the said purpose) as provided under sub-rule (/) of rule 3 of the said rules and 
the performance of Aadhaar authentication for the said purpose shall be on voluntary basis and that the said Agency 
shall perform the Aadhaar authentication only for verifying identity of candidates at various stages of examinations or 
recruitment processes conducted by it, using Yes/No option or eK YC authentication facility. 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred by rule 5 of the said rules read with sub-clause (ii) of 
clause (b) of sub-section (4) of section 4 of the said Act, the said Ministry hereby notifies the following, 
namely: — 


l. The said Agency, as provided in the said Act, shall obtain the consent of the Aadhaar number holder for the 
purpose of authentication herein. 


2. The Aadhaar authentication shall be on voluntary basis in accordance with sub-rule (2) of rule 3 of the said 
rules and the said Agency shall inform to the Aadhaar number holder of the following alternate and viable 


[भाग Ive 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 3, 2025/ज्येष्ठ 0, 947 359 
means of identification and shall not deny any service to the Aadhaar number holder for refusing to, or being 
unable to, undergo Aadhaar authentication, namely: — 

(a) Photo identity 
(b) PAN card 
(c) Voter ID 
3. This notification shall come into force on the date of its publication in the Official Gazette.

पेट्रोलियम और प्राकृतिक गैस मंत्रालय 
नई दिल्‍ली, 24 मई, 2025 


का.आ. 844.--केन्द्रीय सरकार को लोकहित में यह आवश्यक प्रतीत होता है कि पेट्रोलियम पदार्थ परिवहन के 
लिए हिन्दुस्तान पेट्रोलियम कॉर्पोरेशन लिमिटेड द्वारा विसाख (आन्ध्र प्रदेश) से रायपुर (छत्तीसगढ) पाइपलाइन बिछाई 
जानी चाहिए ; 


[भाग ॥---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 3, 2025/ज्येष्ठ 0, 947 3523 


और केन्द्रीय सरकार को ऐसी पाइपलाइन महासमुंद जिला, छतीसगढ राज्य में बिछाने के प्रयोजन के लिए यह 
आवश्यक प्रतीत होता है कि ऐसी भूमि में जो इस से संलग्न अनुसूची में वर्णित है और जिसमें उक्त पाइपलाइन बिछाए जाने 
का प्रस्ताव है, उपयोग के अधिकार का अर्जन किया जाए ; 


अतः अब, केन्द्रीय सरकार, पेट्रोलियम और खनिज पाइपलाइन (भूमि में उपयोग के अधिकार का अर्जन) 
अधिनियम, 962 (7962 का 50) की धारा 3 की उपधारा (॥) द्वारा प्रदत्त शक्तियों का प्रयोग करते हुए, उस भूमि में 
उपयोग के अधिकार का अर्जन करने के अपने आशय की घोषणा करती है ; 


कोई व्यक्ति, जो उक्त अनुसूची में वर्णित भूमि में हितबद्ध है, उस तारीख से जिसको इस अधिसूचना से युक्त भारत 
के राजपत्र की प्रतियाँ साधारण जनता को उपलब्ध करा दी जाती है, इक्कीस दिन के भीतर भूमि के नीचे पाइपलाइन 
बिछाए जाने के लिए उस में उपयोग के अधिकार के अर्जन के सम्बन्ध में सक्षम प्राधिकारी, विसाख - रायपुर पाइपलाइन 
परियोजना, हिन्दुस्तान पेट्रोलियम कॉर्पोरेशन लिमिटेड, भारत सरकार का उपक्रम, सेक्टर-४, हाउस नंबर डी-६४, कमल 
विहार, रायपुर -४९२० ०४, को लिखित रूप में आक्षेप भेज सकेगा।

3564 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 3], 2025/JY AISTHA 0, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS 
New Delhi, the 2lst May, 2025 


S.O. 844.—Whereas, it appears to the Central Government that it is necessary in the public interest that for 
the transportation of Petroleum Product from Visakha (Andhra Pradesh) to Raipur (Chhattisgarh) Pipeline should be 
laid by Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited. 


And whereas, it appears to the Central Government that for the purpose of laying the said pipeline, it is 
necessary to acquire the Right of User in the land under which the said pipeline is proposed to be laid at Mahasamund 
District in Chhattisgarh State, which is described in the Schedule annexed to this notification; 


Now, therefore in exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (l) of section 3 of the Petroleum and 
Minerals Pipelines (Acquisition of Right of User in Land) Act, 962 (50 of 962), the Central Government hereby 
declares its intention to acquire the right of user therein; 


Any person interested in the land described in the said schedule may, within twenty one days from the date 
on which the copies of the Gazette of India containing this notification are made available to the general public, object 
in writing to the acquisition of the right of user therein for laying of the pipeline under the land to The Competent 
Authority, Visakha — Raipur Pipeline Project, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited, Government of India 
Enterprises, Sector-4, House No. 4/D-64, Kamal Vihar, Raipur-492004, Chhattisgarh.

का.आ. 845.--केन्द्रीय सरकार को लोकहित में यह आवश्यक प्रतीत होता है कि पेट्रोलियम पदार्थ परिवहन के 
लिए हिन्दुस्तान पेट्रोलियम कॉर्पोरेशन लिमिटेड द्वारा विसाख (आन्ध्र प्रदेश) से रायपुर (छत्तीसगढ) पाइपलाइन बिछाई 
जानी चाहिए ; 


और केन्द्रीय सरकार को यह पाइपलाइन रायपुर जिला, छतीसगढ राज्य में बिछाने के प्रयोजन के लिए यह 
आवश्यक प्रतीत होता है कि ऐसी भूमि में जो इस से संलग्न अनुसूची में वर्णित है और जिसमें उक्त पाइपलाइन बिछाए जाने 
का प्रस्ताव है, उपयोग के अधिकार का अर्जन किया जाए ; 


अतः अब, केन्द्रीय सरकार, पेट्रोलियम और खनिज पाइपलाइन (भूमि में उपयोग के अधिकार का asta) 
अधिनियम, 962 (7962 का 50) की धारा 3 की उपधारा (॥) द्वारा प्रदत्त शक्तियों का प्रयोग करते हुए, उस भूमि में 
उपयोग के अधिकार का अर्जन करने के अपने आशय की घोषणा करती है ; 


कोई व्यक्ति, जो उक्त अनुसूची में वर्णित भूमि में हितबद्ध है, उस तारीख से जिसको इस अधिसूचना से युक्त भारत 
के राजपत्र की प्रतियाँ साधारण जनता को उपलब्ध करा दी जाती है, इक्कीस दिन के भीतर भूमि के नीचे पाइपलाइन 
बिछाए जाने के लिए उस में उपयोग के अधिकार के अर्जन के सम्बन्ध में सक्षम प्राधिकारी, विसाख - रायपुर पाइपलाइन 
परियोजना, हिन्दुस्तान पेट्रोलियम कॉर्पोरेशन लिमिटेड, भारत सरकार का उपक्रम, सेक्टर-४, हाउस नंबर डी-६४, कमल 
विहार, रायपुर -४९२०१५. को लिखित रूप में आक्षेप भेज सकेगा।

एस.एस.सिंह, अवर सचिव 


New Delhi, the 2lst May, 2025 


S.O. 845.— Whereas, it appears to the Central Government that it is necessary in the public interest that for the 
transportation of Petroleum Product from Visakha (Andhra Pradesh) to Raipur (Chhattisgarh) Pipeline should be laid 
by Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited. 


And whereas, it appears to the Central Government that for the purpose of laying the said pipeline, it is 
necessary to acquire the Right of User in the land under which the said pipeline is proposed to be laid at Raipur 
District in Chhattisgarh State, which is described in the Schedule annexed to this notification; 


Now, therefore in exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section () of section 3 of the Petroleum and Minerals 
Pipelines (Acquisition of Right of User in Land) Act, 962 (50 of 962), the Central Government hereby declares its 
intention to acquire the right of user therein; 


Any person interested in the land described in the said schedule may, within twenty one days from the date on 
which the copies of the Gazette of India containing this notification are made available to the general public, object in 
writing to the acquisition of the right of user therein for laying of the pipeline under the land to The Competent 
Authority, Visakha — Raipur Pipeline Project, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited, Government of India 
Enterprises, Sector-4, House No. 4/D-64, Kamal Vihar, Raipur-49205, Chhattisgarh.

(JUDGMENT) 
(Passed on this 247 day of March - 2025) 


As per letter dated 7.02.2020 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference is 
made to this Tribunal under Section-l0 of Industrial Disputes Act, l947 (in short the ‘Act’)as per Notification 
No. J-(2-)/2020-IR dt. 7.02.2020. The dispute under reference relates to: 


“FAT TATA, वाइस THES, भारतीय इन्फ्राटेल लिमिटेड, गुरूग्राम हरियाण/भारतीय इन्क्राटेल लिमिटेड, इन्दौर AO प्र0/ 
रैण्डस्डेट इण्डिया लिमिटेड, चैन्नई/ रैण्डस्टेड झण्डिया लिमिटेड, इन्दौर म0प्र0 के प्रबंधन व्दारा श्री राजकुमार गौतम आत्मज 
TO रामसेवक गौतम; ATTA टेक्नीशियन को वर्ष 2000 से नियोजन में रखने पश्चात्‌ उसकी सेवाएं 7.2.208 से सामप्त किये जाने 
की PTAA ET TAA है? यदि नहीं तो संबंधित आवेदक किस अनुतोष पाने का हकदार है?” 


Case of the workman is mainly that, he was first appointed by M/s Randstad India Limited in the year 
2000. This company merged into M/s Indus Towers. He worked continuously with M/s Randstad India Ltd. and 
M/s Indus Towers who are the subsidiaries of Bhartiya Infratel Ltd., till 24.2.20l8, when his services were 
terminated by Management without any notice or compensation which is illegal, arbitrary and unjust. The Workman 
has thus prayed that holding the termination of his services against law, he be held entitled to be reinstated with back 
wages and benefits. 


The Management of M/s Indus Towers Ltd. has put up a case that, the Workman was appointed by M/s 
Randstad India Ltd. on contract basis for One year, which was extended on yearly basis till 208. It was found that the 
Workman had obtained this employment by concealing facts, hence to avoid complications, he submitted his 
resignation on 24.!2.208 which was accepted and he was relieved from duty. 


The other managements have not appeared and have not contested the reference. 


During the hearings, the Workman also absented himself, the reference proceeded ex-parte against him. 


3636 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 3, 2025/JY AISTHA 0, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 
Both the sides have filed photocopy documents, which they have not appeared to prove. M/s Indus Towers. 
have filed affidavit of its witness Riya Agrawal. 


At the stage of argument, none was present for the Workman; hence, argument of Mr. Jaydeep Bansal 
Learned Counsel for Management of M/s Indus Towers. was heard by me. No written argument has been filed. I have 
gone through the record. 


The reference itself is the issue for determination in the case in hand. 


The initial burden to prove his case is on the Workman, in which he has failed. Management witness has 
corroborated the case of the Management as stated above. The Photocopy documents also show that the Workman 
was first appointed on 9.0.202 for fixed term of one year which was extended till 20l8. He submitted his 
resignation dated 24.!2.208 which was accepted and he was relieved. Hence, termination of his services cannot be 
said to be illegal or unjust. 


On the basis of above discussion and findings, the reference stands answered against the Workman. 
Holding him entitled to no relief. 


No order as to cost.

(JUDGMENT) 
(Passed on this 25" day of April - 2025) 


The workman has filed this petition under Section 0 (2A) (2&3) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 947, 
hereinafter referred by the word ‘Act’, against the termination of his services by Management of A.S.I. on 30.08.207 
with an allegation that, he was first engaged with the Management at Rinmukteshwar Shiv Mandir Kukramath, 
situated in Distt. DIndori (M.P.) which is maintained by the Archaeological Survey of India on 2004 as a skilled 
worker for its maintenance and worked continuously till 30.08.20l7 when his services were terminated by the 
Superintendent of A.S.I. vide oral order without any notice or compensation which is unjust, illegal and arbitrary 
being in violation of Section 25F and 25G of the Act. His further case is that, he sent various representations to the 
department as well to the Office of PMO and other places but, his grievance was not addressed. Thereafter he raised a 
dispute before the Assistant Labour Commissioner, which could not be conciliated, hence this petition. The Appellant 
has prayed that, setting aside the order of the Management Department dated 30.08.20I7 terminating his services he 
be reinstated with back wages, benefits and also be granted other reliefs thought appropriate by this Tribunal. 


The department has filed a written statement in form of preliminary objection/ reply, wherein they have 
taken a case that the petitioner was engaged as a casual worker for removing the bushes and in other institutional 
works of the Department of Archeological Survey of India, he was not engaged following any recruitment process 
against any sanctioned vacancy, hence he is not entitled to any relief. Other objection taken is that, the department is 
an department under Central Government engaged in Maintenance and Conservation of Ancient Monuments which 
have been taken as Ancient Monuments under the Act, hence, is not engaged in any production and manufacturing 
industry, thus is not an Industry as defined under Section 2(j) of the Act. Also that, since, he has not challenged any 


3638 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 3], 2025/JY AISTHA 0, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


order of his termination or any policy of Government, the dispute is not maintainable before his Tribunal rather he 
should have approached the Central Administrative Tribunal. 


At evidence stage, the petitioner has filed photocopy of Muster Roll, maintained by the Department, 
obtained by him in RTI and has also filed his affidavit as his examination-in-chief over which no cross examination 
has been done by Management. 


Management has not filed any evidence, in form of affidavit or documents. 


It is worth mentioning here that, during the pendency of the case, the Management absented themselves, 
hence, the case was ordered to proceed ex-parte against Management vide order dated 26.!.202] which was recalled 
vide order dated 28.06.2024 on the application by Management on cost. They neither paid the cost nor did they appear 
thereafter. 


I have heard argument of Learned Counsel for the Petitioner Miss. Sushma Pandey. She has filed a 
memorandum of arguments also which is part of record. I have gone through the memorandum of arguments, as well 
the evidences. 


Following issues arises for determination in case in hand — 


I. Whether the Management Department is not an Industry as defined under Section 2(j) of the Act and the 
Dispute is not cognizable by this Tribunal? 


2. Whether the petitioner has successfully proved that, he continuously worked for 240 days, every year 
including the year presiding the date of his termination? 


3. Whether, the order of Management terminating the services of the petitioner is in violation of Section 2577 
and 25G of the Act. 


4. Relief to which the petitioner is entitled? 
Issue No.  - 


As stated by Management in their written objection/reply/ preliminary objection to the petition that since 
they are a Government Department engaged in maintenance and conservation of ancient monuments declared so 
by the Central Government, hence, are not engaged in any manufacturing or production business, thus they are 
not Industry as defined under Section 2(j) of the Act. 


Section 2(j) of the Act is being reproduced as follows: - 


‘Where there is (i) systematic activity, (ii) organized by co-operation between employer and 
employee (the direct and substantial element is chimerical), and (iii) for the production and/ or 
distribution of goods and services calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes (not spiritual or religious 
but inclusive of material things or services granted to celestial bliss e.g. making on a large scale Prasad or 
food), prima facie, there is an ‘industry’ in that enterprise.’ 


Learned Counsel for the petitioner has referred to judgment of Hon’ble High Court of Delhi in the 
case of Archeological Survey of India V.s. P.O. CGIT and Others, W.P. (C ) No. 875%/2075 and CM No. 
5958/2005, Neutral Citation No. 2022/DHC/005746 and Union of India through its Secretary Culture V.s. 
Surendra Singh, reported in AIR Online 2079 All. 653 in support of her argument that, the department is any 
Industry as defined under Section 2(j) of the Act. 


In the cases referred Hon’ble Single Bench of Delhi & Allahabad High Court have relied upon a Seven 
Judge Bench judgment Hon’ble the Supreme Court in the case of the Bangalore Water Supply& Sewage 
Board V.s. Rajappa (978) 2 SCC 23 & other judgments and has held that, the Horticulture section of the 
Archeological Survey of India is not a sovereign identity hence, is Industry as defined under Section 2(j) of the 
Act. In the case in hand, even the department has admitted in their reply that, the Workman was engaged in 
cleaning the bushes in and around the temple and other works regarding maintenance of the temple. The 
Workman has also stated the same in his uncontroverted affidavit as his examination-in-chief. Hence, holding 
the Department an Industry, as defined under Section 2(j) of the Act, in the case in hand. 


Hence Issue ।९४०. is answered accordingly. 
Issue No. 2 & 3 - 
Since these two issues are interconnected, they are being taken together. 
Before any discussion, Section 25(B), 25(F) and 25(G) of the Act are being reproduced as follows: 
25B. Definition of continuous service — 
For the purposes of this Chapter,— 


(7) a workman shall be said to be in continuous service for a period if he is, for that period, in 
uninterrupted service, including service which may be interrupted on account of sickness or authorised 


[भाग वा--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 3, 2025/ज्येष्ठ 0, 947 3639 


leave or an accident or a strike which is not illegal, or a lock-out or a cessation of work which is not due 
to any fault on the part of the workman; 


(2) where a workman is not in continuous service within the meaning of clause (7) for a period of 
one year or six months, he shall be deemed to be in continuous service under an employer— 


(a) for a period of one year, if the workman, during a period of twelve calendar months preceding 
the date with reference to which calculation is to be made, has actually worked under the 
employer for not less than— 


(i) one hundred and ninety days in the case of a workman employed below ground in a 
mine; and 


(ii) two hundred and forty days, in any other case; 


(b) for a period of six months, if the workman, during a period of six calendar months preceding 
the date with reference to which calculation is to be made, has actually worked under the 
employer for not less than— 


(i) ninety-five days, in the case of a workman employed below ground in a mine; and 


(ii) one hundred and twenty days, in any other case. 


25F. Conditions precedent to retrenchment of workmen .— 


No workman employed in any industry who has been in continuous service for not less than one 
year under an employer shall be retrenched by that employer until— 


(a) the workman has been given one month’s notice in writing indicating the reasons for 
retrenchment and the period of notice has expired, or the workman has been paid in lieu of such 
notice, wages for the period of the notice; 


(b) the workman has been paid, at the time of retrenchment, compensation which shall be 
equivalent to fifteen days' average pay [for every completed year of continuous service] or any 
part thereof in excess of six months; and 


(c) notice in the prescribed manner is served on the appropriate Government [or such authority 
as may be specified by the appropriate Government by notification in the Official Gazette. 


25G. Procedure for retrenchment.— 


Where any workman in an industrial establishment, who is a citizen of India, is to be retrenched 
and he belongs to a particular category of workmen in that establishment, in the absence of any 
agreement between the employer and the workman in this behalf, the employer shall ordinarily retrench 
the workman who was the last person to be employed in that category, unless for reasons to be recorded 
the employer retrenches any other workman. 


It is the case of Workman that he had been working with the Management since 2004 till date of 
termination of his services i.e. on 30.08.20I7 he has filed his affidavit in support of his this allegation which is 
uncontroverted, this affidavit is further corroborated by the copy of Muster Roll filed by the petitioner Workman and 
also the Department does not specifically dispute this allegation in their pleadings/ reply lead to a conclusion that the 
Workman has successfully proved his continuous service as defined under Section 25(B) of the Act. 


Learned Counsel has referred to following judgment in this respect :- 
Workmen of American Expresss V.s. Management of American Express, (79865) 4 SCC 77. 
Employers in relation to Dighwadih V.s. Their Workmen AIR (7966) SC 75. 


It is the case of the Workman that, he has not been issued any notice nor has been paid any compensation 
on termination of his services which is corroborated by his uncontroverted affidavit. There is no pleading or prove by 
the Department rebutting this allegation, hence, termination of his services by the Department is held in violation of 
Section 25(F) and 25(G) of the Act. 


Issue No. 2 & 3 are answered accordingly. 
Issue No. 4 — 


Learned Counsel for workman has submitted that, it is a fit case for reinstatement of the Workman, with full 
back-wages and benefits. Learned Counsel further submits that, the department engaged him for as many as |3 years, 
which shows that, the Workman was on permanent and perennial nature which is regarding the maintenance activities 
in the Temple. The Work is still available and also that, the Management Department has engaged in unfair labour 
practice as defined under Section 2 (r a) of the Act, which is prohibited under the Act. Leaned Counsel further

submits that, the job for which the petitioner was employed is of manual nature for which no educational qualification 
is required, hence, to undo the unfair labour practice adopted by Management department in the case in hand; only 
reinstatement of the Workman with back-wages will meet the ends of justice. 


Learned Counsel has referred to following judgment in this respect :- 


Goverdhan V.s. Chief Municipal Officer Misc. Petition No. 6329/2022 Hon’ble High Court of M.P. 


“In this case, the Workman had worked for 8 years, as a Labour with the Department, a Single Bench of 
Hon’ble High Court confirmed order of his reinstatement in services with 50% back wages and consequential 
benefits.” 


Section 2 (r a) 5" Schedule is being reproduced as follows : 
“Unfair Labour Practice on part of Employers.- 


0. to employ workmen as badlis, casuals, or temporaries and to continue them with as such for years, 
with the object of depriving them of status and privileges of permanent workmen.” 


It is established from the fact of the case in hand that, the department has kept the petitioner workman as 
daily wager, for as many as |3 years. The soul aim of which can be assumed is for the purpose of depriving him the 
benefits of the permanent status and has adopted unfair labour practice which is prohibited in the Act and is 
punishable as a Crime as well. 


Following observations of Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Jaggo V.s. Union of India and Others. 
SLP (c) No. 5580 of 2024 are being mentioned as follows :- 


8. On behalf of the appellants, the following arguments have been advanced before us: 


(i). Continuous and Substantive Engagement: The appellants emphasize their long, uninterrupted service spanning 
well over a decade-and in some instances, exceeding two decades. They argue that their duties were neither sporadic 
nor project-based but permanent and integral to the daily functioning of the respondent's offices. 


(ii). Nature of Duties: Their responsibilities- such as cleaning, dusting, gardening, and other maintenance tasks-were 
not casual or peripheral. Instead, they were central to ensuring a clean, orderly, and functional work environment, 
effectively aligning with roles typically associated with regular posts. 


(iii). Absence of Performance Issues: Throughout their tenure, the appellants were never issued any warning or 
adverse remarks. They highlight that their work was consistently satisfactory, and there was no indication from the 
respondents that their performance was not satisfactory or required improvement. 


(iv). Compliance with 'Uma Devi' Guidelines: The appellants assert that their appointments were not "illegal" but at 
most "irregular." Drawing on the principles laid down in Secretary, State of Karnataka vs. Uma Devi4, they submit 
that long-serving employees in irregular appointments-who fulfil essential, sanctioned functions-are entitled to 
consideration for regularization. 


(v). Discrimination in Regularization: The appellants point out that individuals with fewer years of service or similar 
engagements have been regularized. They contend that denying them the same benefit, despite their longer service 
and crucial role, constitutes arbitrary and discriminatory treatment. 


(vi). Irrelevance of Educational Qualifications: The appellants reject the respondents' reliance on formal 
educational requirements, noting that such criteria were never enforced earlier and that the nature of their work does 
not inherently demand formal schooling. They argue that retrospectively imposing such qualifications is unjustified 
given their proven capability over many years. 


(vii). Equity and Fairness: Ultimately, the appellants submit that the High Court erred by focusing too rigidly on 
their initial terms of engagement and ignoring the substantive reality of their long, integral service. They maintain 
that fairness, equity, and established judicial principles call for their regularization rather than abrupt termination 


9. On the other hand, the following primary arguments have been advanced before us on behalf of the Respondents: 


(i). Nature of Engagement: The respondents maintain that the appellants were engaged purely on a part-time, 
contractual basis, limited to a few hours a day, and that their work was never intended to be permanent or full-time. 


(ii). Absence of Sanctioned Posts: They assert that the appellants were not appointed against any sanctioned posts. 
According to the respondents, without sanctioned vacancies, there can be no question of regularization or absorption 
into the permanent workforce. 


(iii). Non-Compliance with 'Uma Devi' Criteria: Relying heavily on Secretary, State of Karnataka vs. Uma Devi 
(supra), the respondents argue that the appellants do not meet the conditions necessary for regularization. They 
emphasize that merely serving a long period on a part-time or ad-hoc basis does not create a right to be regularized. 


(iv). Educational Qualifications: The respondents contend that even if the appellants were to be considered for 
regular appointments, they do not possess the minimum educational qualifications mandated for regular recruitment. 


[भाग त---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 3, 2025/ज्येष्ठ 0, 947 364] 


This, in their view, disqualifies the appellants from being absorbed into regular service. 


(v). Outsourcing as a Legitimate Policy Decision: The respondents point out that they have chosen to outsource the 
relevant housekeeping and maintenance work to a private agency. This, they argue, is a legitimate administrative 
policy decision aimed at improving efficiency and cannot be interfered with by the courts. 


(vi). No Fundamental Right to Regularization: Finally, the respondents underscore that no employee, merely by 
virtue of long-standing temporary or parttime engagement, acquires a vested right to be regularized. They maintain 
that the appellants’ claims are devoid of any legal entitlement and that the High Court was correct in dismissing their 
petition. 


409. Having given careful consideration to the submissions advanced and the material on record, we find that the 
appellants' long and uninterrupted service, for periods extending well beyond ten years, cannot be brushed aside 
merely by labelling their initial appointments as part-time or contractual. The essence of their employment must be 
considered in the light of their sustained contribution, the integral nature of their work, and the fact that no evidence 
suggests their entry was through any illegal or surreptitious route. 


4. The appellants, throughout their tenure, were engaged in performing essential duties that were indispensable to 
the day-to-day functioning of the offices of the Central Water Commission (CWC). Applicant Nos. I, 2, and 3, as 
Safaiwalis, were responsible for maintaining hygiene, cleanliness, and a conducive working environment within the 
office premises. Their duties involved sweeping, dusting, and cleaning of floors, workstations, and common areas-a 
set of responsibilities that directly contributed to the basic operational functionality of the CWC. Applicant No. 5, in 
the role of a Khallasi (with additional functions akin to those of a Mali), was entrusted with critical maintenance 
tasks, including gardening, upkeep of outdoor premises, and ensuring orderly surroundings. 


2. Despite being labelled as "part-time workers," the appellants performed these essential tasks on a daily and 
continuous basis over extensive periods, ranging from over a decade to nearly two decades. Their engagement was 
not sporadic or temporary in nature; instead, it was recurrent, regular, and akin to the responsibilities typically 
associated with sanctioned posts. Moreover, the respondents did not engage any other personnel for these tasks 
during the appellants’ tenure, underscoring the indispensable nature of their work. 


उ., The claim by the respondents that these were not regular posts lacks merit, as the nature of the work performed by 
the appellants was perennial and fundamental to the functioning of the offices. The recurring nature of these duties 
necessitates their classification as regular posts, irrespective of how their initial engagements were labelled. It is also 
noteworthy that subsequent outsourcing of these same tasks to private agencies after the appellants’ termination 
demonstrates the inherent need for these services. This act of outsourcing, which effectively replaced one set of 
workers with another, further underscores that the work in question was neither temporary nor occasional. 


4, The abrupt termination of the appellants’ services, following dismissal of their Original Application before the 
Tribunal, was arbitrary and devoid of any justification. The termination letters, issued without prior notice or 
explanation, violated fundamental principles of natural justice. It is a settled principle of law that even contractual 
employees are entitled to a fair hearing before any adverse action is taken against them, particularly when their 
service records are unblemished. In this case, the appellants were given no opportunity to be heard, nor were they 
provided any reasons for their dismissal, which followed nearly two decades of dedicated service. 


I5. Furthermore, the respondents’ conduct in issuing tenders for outsourcing the same tasks during the pendency of 
judicial proceedings, despite a stay order from the Tribunal directing maintenance of status quo, reveals lack of bona 
fide intentions. Such actions not only contravened judicial directives but also underscored the respondents' 
unwillingness to acknowledge the appellants’ rightful claims to regularization. 


46. The appellants’ consistent performance over their long tenures further solidifies their claim for regularization. At 
no point during their engagement did the respondents raise any issues regarding their competence or performance. 
On the contrary, their services were extended repeatedly over the years, and their remuneration, though minimal, was 
incrementally increased which was an implicit acknowledgment of their satisfactory performance. The respondents' 
belated plea of alleged unsatisfactory service appears to be an afterthought and lacks credibility. 


47. As for the argument relating to educational qualifications, we find it untenable in the present context. The nature 
of duties the appellants performed-cleaning, sweeping, dusting, and gardening-does not inherently mandate formal 
educational prerequisites. It would be unjust to rely on educational criteria that were never central to their 
engagement or the performance of their duties for decades. 


Moreover, the respondents themselves have, by their conduct, shown that such criteria were not strictly enforced in 
other cases of regularization. The appellants’ long-standing satisfactory performance itself attests to their capability 
to discharge these functions, making rigid insistence on formal educational requirements an unreasonable hurdle. 


36. The appellants have also established that individuals with lesser tenure or comparable roles were regularized by 
the respondents. The counsel for the appellants had submitted a seniority list for employees working as the Multi-

the staff without the required educational qualification:

A bare perusal of the aforementioned list shows the preferential treatment accorded to these individuals, despite their 
shorter service durations and no educational qualification. This exemplifies discriminatory behaviour and lack of 
uniformity in the respondent department's approach. Such disparity violates the principles of equality enshrined in 
Articles /4 and I6 of the Constitution of India and cannot be sustained in law. 


49, It is evident from the foregoing that the appellants’ roles were not only essential but also indistinguishable from 
those of regular employees. Their sustained contributions over extended periods, coupled with absence of any adverse 
record, warrant equitable treatment and regularization of their services. Denial of this benefit, followed by their 
arbitrary termination, amounts to manifest injustice and must be rectified. 


20. It is well established that the decision in Uma Devi (supra) does not intend to penalize employees who have 
rendered long years of service fulfilling ongoing and necessary functions of the State or its instrumentalities. The said 
judgment sought to prevent backdoor entries and illegal appointments that circumvent constitutional requirements. 


However, where appointments were not illegal but possibly "irregular," and where employees had served 
continuously against the backdrop of sanctioned functions for a considerable period, the need for a fair and humane 
resolution becomes paramount. Prolonged, continuous, and unblemished service performing tasks inherently required 
on a regular basis can, over the time, transform what was initially ad-hoc or temporary into a scenario demanding 
fair regularization. 


In a recent judgement of this Court in Vinod Kumar and Ors. Etc. Vs. Union of India & Ors.5, it was held that held 
that procedural formalities cannot be used to deny regularization of service to an employee whose appointment was 
termed "temporary" but has performed the same duties as performed by the regular employee over a considerable 
period in the capacity of the regular employee. The relevant paras of this judgement have been reproduced below: 


"6. The application of the judgment in Uma Devi (supra) by the High Court does not fit squarely with the facts at 
hand, given the specific circumstances under which the appellants were employed and have continued their service. 
The reliance on procedural formalities at the outset cannot be used to perpetually deny substantive rights that have 
accrued over a considerable period through continuous service. Their promotion was based on a specific notification 
for vacancies and a subsequent circular, followed by a selection process involving written tests and interviews, which 
distinguishes their case from the appointments through back door entry as discussed in the case of Uma Devi (supra). 


7. The judgement in the case Uma Devi (supra) also distinguished between "irregular" and "illegal" appointments 
underscoring the importance of considering certain appointments even if were not made strictly in accordance with 
the prescribed Rules and Procedure, cannot be said to have been made illegally if they had followed the procedures 
of regular appointments such as conduct of written examinations or interviews as in the present case." 


24. The High Court placed undue emphasis on the initial label of the appellants' engagements and the outsourcing 


[भाग त---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 3, 2025/ज्येष्ठ 0, 947 3643 


decision taken after their dismissal. Courts must look beyond the surface labels and consider the realities of 
employment: continuous, long-term service, indispensable duties, and absence of any mala fide or illegalities in their 
appointments. In that light, refusing regularization simply because their original terms did not explicitly state so, or 
because an outsourcing policy was belatedly introduced, would be contrary to principles of fairness and equity. 


22. The pervasive misuse of temporary employment contracts, as exemplified in this case, reflects a broader systemic 
issue that adversely affects workers’ rights and job security. In the private sector, the rise of the gig economy has led 
to an increase in precarious employment arrangements, often characterized by lack of benefits, job security, and fair 
treatment. 


Such practices have been criticized for exploiting workers and undermining labour standards. Government 
institutions, entrusted with upholding the principles of fairness and justice, bear an even greater responsibility to 
avoid such exploitative employment practices. When public sector entities engage in misuse of temporary contracts, it 
not only mirrors the detrimental trends observed in the gig economy but also sets a concerning precedent that can 
erode public trust in governmental operations. 


23. The International Labour Organization (ILO), of which India is a founding member, has consistently advocated 
for employment stability and the fair treatment of workers. The ILO's Multinational Enterprises Declaration6 
encourages companies to provide stable employment and to observe obligations concerning employment stability and 
social security. It emphasizes that enterprises should assume a leading role in promoting employment security, 
particularly in contexts where job discontinuation could exacerbate long-term unemployment. 


24. The landmark judgement of the United State in the case of Vizcaino v. Microsoft Corporation7 serves as a 
pertinent example from the private sector, illustrating the consequences of misclassifying employees to circumvent 
providing benefits. In this case, Microsoft classified certain workers as independent contractors, thereby denying 
them employee benefits. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit determined that these workers were, in fact, 
common-law employees and were entitled to the same benefits as regular employees. 


The Court noted that large Corporations have increasingly adopted the practice of hiring temporary employees or 
independent contractors as a means of avoiding payment of employee benefits, thereby increasing their profits. This 
judgment underscores the principle that the nature of the work performed, rather than the label assigned to the 
worker, should determine employment status and the corresponding rights and benefits. It highlights the judiciary's 
role in rectifying such misclassifications and ensuring that workers receive fair treatment. 


25. It is a disconcerting reality that temporary employees, particularly in government institutions, often face 
multifaceted forms of exploitation. While the foundational purpose of temporary contracts may have been to address 
short-term or seasonal needs, they have increasingly become a mechanism to evade longterm obligations owed to 
employees. These practices manifest in several ways: 


e Misuse of "Temporary" Labels: Employees engaged for work that is essential, recurring, and integral to 
the functioning of an institution are often labeled as "temporary" or "contractual," even when their roles 
mirror those of regular employees. Such misclassification deprives workers of the dignity, security, and 
benefits that regular employees are entitled to, despite performing identical tasks. 


e Arbitrary Termination: Temporary employees are frequently dismissed without cause or notice, as seen in 
the present case. This practice undermines the principles of natural justice and subjects workers to a state of 
constant insecurity, regardless of the quality or duration of their service. 


e Lack of Career Progression: Temporary employees often find themselves excluded from opportunities for 
skill development, promotions, or incremental pay raises. They remain stagnant in their roles, creating a 
systemic disparity between them and their regular counterparts, despite their contributions being equally 
significant. 


e Using Outsourcing as a Shield: Institutions increasingly resort to outsourcing roles performed by 
temporary employees, effectively replacing one set of exploited workers with another. This practice not only 
perpetuates exploitation but also demonstrates a deliberate effort to bypass the obligation to offer regular 
employment. 


e Denial of Basic Rights and Benefits: Temporary employees are often denied fundamental benefits such as 
pension, provident fund, health insurance, and paid leave, even when their tenure spans decades. This lack 
of social security subjects them and their families to undue hardship, especially in cases of illness, 
retirement, or unforeseen circumstances. 


26. While the judgment in Uma Devi (supra) sought to curtail the practice of backdoor entries and ensure 
appointments adhered to constitutional principles, it is regrettable that its principles are often misinterpreted or 
misapplied to deny legitimate claims of long-serving employees. This judgment aimed to distinguish between "illegal" 
and "irregular" appointments. It categorically held that employees in irregular appointments, who were engaged in 
duly sanctioned posts and had served continuously for more than ten years, should be considered for regularization 


3644 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 3, 2025/JY AISTHA 0, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


as a one-time measure. 


However, the laudable intent of the judgment is being subverted when institutions rely on its dicta to indiscriminately 
reject the claims of employees, even in cases where their appointments are not illegal, but merely lack adherence to 
procedural formalities. Government departments often cite the judgment in Uma Devi (supra) to argue that no vested 
right to regularization exists for temporary employees, overlooking the judgment's explicit acknowledgment of cases 
where regularization is appropriate. This selective application distorts the judgment's spirit and purpose, effectively 
weaponizing it against employees who have rendered indispensable services over decades. 


27. In light of these considerations, in our opinion, it is imperative for government departments to lead by example in 
providing fair and stable employment. Engaging workers on a temporary basis for extended periods, especially when 
their roles are integral to the organization's functioning, not only contravenes international labour standards but also 
exposes the organization to legal challenges and undermines employee morale. 


By ensuring fair employment practices, government institutions can reduce the burden of unnecessary litigation, 
promote job security, and uphold the principles of justice and fairness that they are meant to embody. This approach 
aligns with international standards and sets a positive precedent for the private sector to follow, thereby contributing 
to the overall betterment of labour practices in the country. 


The facts of the case are identical to the cases referred. 


Hence in the light of above discussion, the petitioner workman is held entitled to be reinstated, keeping in 
view the fact he is alleged with that he is not being in gainful employment after termination of his services till date 
and has corroborated this fact in his uncorroborated affidavit hence, holding that, the petitioner is not being in gainful 
employment form the date of his termination, he is held entitled to back wages from the date of termination of his 
services till he is reinstated and also entitled to consequential benefits with respect to consideration of permanent 
status and regularization of his services as per relevant rules. 


Issue No. 4 is answered accordingly. 
ORDER 


Holding the action of department in terminating the services of the petitioner workman Satish Kumar 
Pandey on 30.08.207, unjust, arbitrary and illegal, he is entitled to be reinstated with back wages. He is also 
held entitled to for consideration of granting permanent status and regularization as per rules. 


No order as to cost.

(JUDGMENT) 


(Passed on this 09'"day of April- 2025) 


As per letter dated 25/04/206 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference is 
made to this Tribunal under Section-l0 of Industrial Disputes Act, 947 (in short the ‘Act’)as per Notification No. L- 
4202/49/206 (IR(DU)) dt. 25/04/206. The dispute under reference relates to: 


“Whether the action of the management of Central Farm Machinery Training & Testing Institute in 
terminating the service of the workman Shri Radhakrishan Kewat, S/o Shri Hridhayram Kewat, w.e.f. 22.08.2005 
is illegal, arbitrary and violation of the Section 257 of the ID Act, 79472 If yes, to what relief the workman is 
entitled to and from which date?” 


On the basis of reference, notices were issued to the parties. They appeared and filed their respective 
statements of defense and claims. 


Case of the Workman is mainly that, he was appointed after interview by Management on the post of 
Peon/ Gardener on 0!.0.993 as a permanent employee, and worked continuously till 22.08.2005, when his services 
were terminated by Management without any notice or compensation or any enquiry. The Work taken by him by 
Management is of permanent nature. According to the Workman this action of management is unjust, illegal and 
arbitrary. 


Case of Management is mainly that, the Workman was engaged as a Labour on casual basis and as when 
required and was paid daily wages. He was not appointed against any sanctioned post following recruitment 
procedure. He was initially employed as Casual Labour on 0.09.992 on Daily Rate Basis, was granted temporary 
status in accordance with the scheme called Casual Labourers (Grant of Temporary Status and Regularization) 
Scheme of Government of India, 7993 vide order dated 2|.07.984. He was irregular in his presence on duty, used to 
misbehave with Officers and Clerks and was also involved in many incidents of misconduct, dereliction of duty, and 
theft of the property of the Institute. Letters on 23.05.]995, 3.0.207, and 03.05.2000 were issued to him directing 
him to improve his conduct, also oral warnings were issued to him from time to time. He was found drunk on duty 
and a show-cause notice dated 7.08.2005 was issued to him in this respect. He submitted his explanation on 
8.08.2005 in which he admitted the charges, and assured not to repeat it further. His case was reviewed by a 
Committee of Officials and considering his past conduct in Five years, Management decided to disengage him from 
his services. He has raised this dispute after Nine years from the date of his dismissal on 22.08.2005. According to 
Management, their action is just in law. 


In evidence, the Workman filed his affidavit as his examination-in-chief. No cross-examination was done 


3646 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 3, 2025/JY AISTHA 0, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


by Management. The Workman did not file any document. 


Management filed photocopy of Grant of Temporary Status Rules, Office Order granting Temporary Status 
to Workman and Photocopy reference admitted by Workman, hence marked as Exhibits. Rest of the photocopy 
documents are Enquiry Order of Management dated 23.05.995, issuing of warning by Management, show cause 
notice dated 3.0I.997, 03.05.200l. I7.08.2005, Admission of misconduct by Workman vide his letter dated 
8.08.2005 report of Review Committee, order dated !9.08.2005 regarding dismissal of the Workman but these 
documents have been not admitted by Workman side and Management did not care to prove these documents. 


Management did not care to appear and contest the case after filing Written Statement. They did not file 
evidence of any Witness. 


At the time of argument also, Learned Counsel for Management did not appear, hence arguments of 
Learned Counsel for Workman Shri. R.B. Tiwari was heard. No written arguments have been filed by any of the 
patties, in spite of opportunity given. 

I have gone through the record in the light of arguments. 

The reference itself is the issue for determination. 


Undisputed in the pleadings is the fact that, the Workman worked continuously from 993 to 2005, firstly, 
as Casual Labour and thereafter, as a Temporary Worker since 994. Case of Management is that, his services were 
dispensed with and he was disengaged on the basis of some misconduct which he himself admitted. Documents in this 
respect have been filed by Management which have been not been admitted by Workman. Hence, the burden was on 
Management to prove this documents and their case in their Written Statement. On the other side, there is a 
uncontroverted affidavit of Workman that he was disengaged without notice or compensation. Hence, holding his 
disengagement in this circumstances as retrenchment as defined under Section 2 (00) of the Act. This Act of 
Management is held in violation of Section 25(F) and 25(G) of the Act because of none payment of retrenchment 
compensation and notice pay. 


As regards relief, the Workman was a Temporary Labour, hence his retrenchment in this circumstances as 
mentioned above will not sufficiently serve in the interest of justice. After considering all the facts and circumstances 
of the Case in hand as mentioned above, a lump sum compensation of Rs. 50,000/- in lieu of his claims will be 
justified in law, to which the Workman is held entitled to get from Management within 30 days from date of 
publication of Award, failing which interest @ 6% per annum. 


The reference stands answered accordingly.

AWARD 


(Passed on this 2“ day of April-2025.) 


As per letter dated 5/09/205 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference is 
received. The reference is made to this tribunal under section-l0 of ID. Act, l947 as per reference number L- 
4202/47/205 IR(DU) dt. [5/09/205. The dispute under reference related to :- 


“Whether the action of the management of Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd., Bhopal in terminating the 
services of workman Smt. Kiran W/o. Prabhu Lal w.e.f. 0.0.203 is justified ? If not, what relief the 
workman is entitled to ? 


After registering the case on reference received, notices were sent to the parties and were duly served on 
them. They appeared and filed their respective statements of claim and defense. 


The workman has alleged that her husband was a permanent employee of the management. He lost his vision 
and was compulsorily retired on medical basis by management vide order dated 04.06.996. She was engaged by 
management in his place being his wife and worked till 0.2.203 when she was terminated by management without 
notice or compensation which is unjust, illegal and arbitrary. 


Management has taken a case that, she was employed by contractor and was working as an outsourced 
employee in the premises of management. Her services were terminated by contractor. 


In evidence, the workman has filed her affidavit which is uncontroverted. Management has also filed 
affidavit of its witness which is uncontroverted. 


I have heard argument of learned Counsel for workman Mr. Ashok Shrivastava. None appeared for 
management at the stage of argument. Parties have not filed any written arguments. I have gone through the record. 


The initial burden to prove her case is on the workman. Only herself serving affidavit cannot be held to be 
sufficient in absence of any other documentary evidence to hold that she has discharged her this burden. 


Hence, holding that the workman could not prove her case, the reference deserves to be answered 
against her and is answered accordingly. 


No order as to cost.

of Labour & Employment, New Delhi, orderNo.L-!02/06/208-IR(CM-I) dated 24.07.208 .Theterms of reference 
given in the schedule are as follows: 


“Whether the action of the Management of Air India Limited, Mumbai in (i) Unilaterally introducing interchangeabili

ty of the job functions of the Male Flight Pursers with that of Female Air Hostess,

(iii) Unilateral assignment of the flight duties during the bilateral rest period, (iv) Marking of absenteeism fromduty

2. At the outset it is required to mention here that this Tribunal had answered the reference in favour of 22 workmen 
out of total [34 workmen for their regularization under the management of Block-II Area of M/s. BCCL, Dhanbad 
vide Award dated 8.2.207. 


3.The management of Block-II Area of M/s. BCCL, Dhanbad has preferred writ petition before the Hon’ble 
Jharkhand High Court, Ranchi against the award passed by this Tribunal and the Hon’ble Jharkhand High Court has 
been pleased to set aside the Award vide W.P.(L) No. 3425 of 208 dated 22.0.2024 for passing a fresh award with 
respect to 22 workmen without being influenced by any observation or finding recorded in the impugned award 


4 After receipt of the order of the Hon’ble Jharkhand High Court on 02.2.2024 the case was restored to the 
original file. 


5.The case of the Bihar Colliery Kamgar Union as per its written statement is as follows:- 


that altogether 34 workmen had been working under the Kassergara Siding under the Management of BCCL since 
long with unblemished record in a permanent nature of job under the direct control and supervision of the BCCL 
Management. They were performing the job of shale picking, lump coal breaking, line cleaning, removal of stone etc. 
The coal raised from Jamunia and Nud Khurkee Collieries were transported to Kessergara siding for its loading into 
the wagons. The management of BCCL had implemented the Wage Board Recommendation and as per 
recommendation they were entitled for regularization under Category-I. They were performing the same and similar 
nature of work as performed by the other workmen of management of M/s. BCCL who were getting wages of 
Category-I but the management of BCCL had been paying them Rs. 52.50/ per workmen per day which was 
less than the prescribed CategoryI wages in the name of different intermediaries which was nothing but a legal camo 
uflage. The management had been disbursing their wages in the name of intermediaries to create a smoke screen and t 
he management had created a perfect paper arrangement to conceal the real fact which was not genuine. They had rep 
resented with the help of Union before the Management on several times for their regularization and payment of wage 
s of Categoryl wages in view of several decisions of Hon’ble Supreme Court and Hon’ble High Court but no action h 
ad been taken. Subsequently the union has raised a dispute before the Assistant Labour Commissioner (Central), Dhan 
bad but the same ended in failure due to the adamant attitude of the management. 


A prayer has been made to regularize all the workmen namely Sri Karma Mahato and (33 others under the 
management of BCCL. 


6.On the other hand the case of the management, in brief, as per its written statement is as follows:- 


that there had been no employeremployee relationship between the management and the concerned workmen. The 
concerned workmen were working under the transport contractor and some of them are job seekers, who combined 
together for keeping themselves recorded with the help of litigation. The management had allotted contract to 
transport contactors from time to time for transporting coal from the colliery depot to the Railway siding and loading 
the same into wagons. The transport contractors deployed pay loaders for loading coal into dumpers which 
transported the coal and mechanically unloaded at the Kessurgarh Railway siding. The loading of the coal into the 
Railway wagons was done by pay loaders, so the transport contractors was loading coal with the help of pay loaders 
and was transportating coal by dumpers or other vehicles, so the manual labour was not required, save and except, the 
operations of dumpers. The management had not engaged any manual labour on the job of loading, unloading of coal 
or any other job which comes within the prohibited category as per provisions of Section 0 of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, !970. The lumpy coal coming out from the mine passed through feeder breakers and 
the lumpy coal was prepared into proper sizes mechanically and thereafter loaded into the dumpers by pay loaders of 
the contractor for transportation to Kessurgarh Railway siding, so there was no requirement of engaging any shale 
pickers as the coal was processed at the colliery siding where the shale pickers were engaged to pick out the shale and 
the stone from the dump. The contractor was required to ensure loading of coal, free from stone and shale and in that 
connection the contractor had engaged few persons as and when required for the purpose of picking shale and stone in

the process of loading. The jobs of shale pickers was casual in nature and maintenance of quality had been the 
responsibility of the contractor, so some of the concerned workmen might had worked as shale pickers on casual basis 
as and when required under him but such a large number of workmen were never deployed on the job of shale pickers 
under the contractor. The management had sufficient number of shale pickers and other casual workers to do the jobs 
of cleaning the track lines or removing of stone and other materials to clear the movement of the Railway Wagons. 
The concerned workmen had never the workmen of the management and they were not selected or recruited by the

FINDINGS 


2. At the outset of discussion it is required to mention here that union/workmen have raised this dispute regarding 
regularization of services of !34 workmen by the management of Block-II Area of M/s. BCCL on the ground of their 
continuous service of Shale Picking, Lump Coal Breaking, Line Cleaning and Removal of stone etc for last 20 years. 
However the management of BCCL has categorically denied about the relationship of employeremployee existing 
between the concerned workmen and the management of BCCL on the ground that the management had allotted 
contract work to transport contractors for transporting coal from colliery depot to Railway Siding and loading the 
same into wagons, so they had not engaged the concerned workmen. 


3. Now, first of all, this Tribunal thinks it proper to discuss and analyze the oral and documentary evidence available 
on the record. The WW-I, Shanti Devi is one of the concerned workwomen who has deposed that she and other 
workmen had been working in Kessergraha Siding of Block IT Area for more then 20 years continuously under the 
direct control and supervision of the management. She has also stated that the said job of Shale Picking, Lump Coal 
Breaking, Line Cleaning and Removal of Stone etc was permanent and continuous nature of job under the direct 
control and supervision of the management. She has also deposed that she and other workmen had been paid less 
wages in comparison with the workers of Cat-I who were paid wages by the management as per NCWA. She has also 
deposed that under the camouflage of contract/intermediaries the management of BCCL had engaged them but their 
services are not being regularized even after continuous service of 20 years. She has claimed regularization of 
services of her and other workmen as a Shale Picker under Cat-I as per NCWA with prospective effect. In the 
crossexamination she has deposed that she has no appointment letter but she can file the letter of Narula Saheb an 
officer of BCCL. She has also deposed that she and other workmen were gettingwages from BCCL. 


4. The concerned workman has proved the photo copies of pass book of CMPF of 22 workmen out of 34 workmen 
which is marked as Exhibit ऐश analyzing the photo copies of all the passbook of CMPF it appears that the same 
has been attested by the Mines Manager in the year 20l6 whereas the claim for the present reference case is of the 
year 995. It further appears that these passbooks do not show that they have been issued by competent authorities of 
Coal Mines Provident Fund. Further the copies of all the passbooks of workmen show that there is a deposit of 
contribution amount of members as well as employers for one year only. It is relevant to mention here that in one of 
the passbooks the date of birth of workman, namely Sapan Bauri, has been mentioned as 05.0.985 and the reference 
has been received by this Tribunal in the year 4995 after failure of conciliation before the labour authorities which 
means that the said workman Sapan Bauri was performing his duty either the age of 0 or before that, which does not 
seems probable. Further after going through the pass-book of Lato Ravidas it appears that his pass book has been 
attested in the year 20l6 in which his date of birth has been mentioned as l8 years whereas reference has been 
received by this Tribunal in the year [995, which means the workman Lato Ravidas was performing his duties before 
his birth, which is not probable. Moreover, in the passbook of Shanti Devi it appears that her passbook has been 
attested in the year 207 in which her date of birth has been mentioned as I[5 years whereas reference has been 
received in the year !995, which means the workwoman Shanti Devi was performing her duties before her birth, 
which is not probable. Further, in the passbook of Somari Devi it appears that her pass-book has been attested in the 
year 206 in which her date of birth has been mentioned as 29 years whereas reference has been received in the year 
995, which means the workwoman Somari Devi was performing her duty at either the age of 8 or before that, which 
is not probable. In the passbook of Chandra Shekhar Mahato it appears that his pass-book has_ been attested in the 
year 20|7 in which his date of birth has been mentioned as year 997 whereas reference has been received in the year 
995, which means the workman Chandra Shekhar Mahato was performing his duty after two years of his birth, 
which is not probable. 


5. After thoroughly examining all the Pass-Books of Exhibit W | Series, the Tribunal finds that there are lots of 
discrepancies and as such these pass-books are not reliable. 


3668 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 3], 2025/JY AISTHA 0, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


6. At this stage it is relevant to mention the definition of employee as mentioned in Coal Mines Provident Fund And 
Miscellaneous Provisions Act as per Section 2 (d) “employee” means any person who is employed for wages in any 
kind of work, manual or otherwise, in or in connection with a coal mine, and who gets his wages directly or indirectly 
from the employer, and includes — 


(I)any person employed by or through a contractor in or in connection with a coal mine, 
ONE (2) octet 0०००४ eset ta 


7. Now, after going through the definition of employee under Coal Mines Provident Fund and Miscellaneous 
Provisions Act it is clear that if any person is getting wages from the contractor, he or she will be an employee under 
Coal Mines Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act. 


8.It is important to mention here that the concerned workmen/union has not produced or filed any documents except 
the passbook of the CMPF regarding their appointment by the management of BCCL. Further they have not filed any 
documents showing payment of wages by the management of BCCL. 


9. On the other hand the MW-I, Benedict Xalxo has categorically deposed that the concerned workmen were never 
engaged by the management from for breaking, shale picking or any job under the management. He has also deposed 
that the management had allotted contract works to transport contractor from time to time for transportation of coal 
from colliery depot to the railway siding and loading the same into wagons at Kessergraha Railway Siding. In the 
crossexamination he has deposed that the Shale Picker work was done by the contractor by its workers and 
contractors are engaged by the management. He has also deposed that there is no Shale Picker designation in 
Kessergraha Railway Siding and Shale Picker are Catl workman. The management has proved the work order for 
transportation of coal in BlockII Area of the period 99I, 992, [993 and 995 which are marked as Exhibit । 
series. Further the management had proved the work order of the year 989, [992, 993 and 995 to other contractors 
for transportation of coal. On perusal of Exhibit M-I series it appears that work order for transportation of coal from 
different sources of BlockII Area of different places of coal dispatches loading of wagons has been issued. The 
Exhibit M-2, M 3, M4, M5 and M6 are also letters issued by General Manager to different contractors for 
transportation of coal from different sources of Block-II Area to other places. 


20.Now, after analyzing the documents of Exhibit M-I series, M-2, M-3, M-4, M-5 and M 6 it appears that the 
management had allotted the work of coal transportation to the contractor for transporting coal from the different 
sources of Blok-II Area to different places of dispatch. 


2l. At this stage it is relevant to mention here, the decision of Hon’ble Supreme Court passed in Balwant Rai Saluja 
vs. Air India Ltd., (204) 9 SCC 407, in which the Hon’ble Supreme Court has been pleased to hold that the “relevant 
factors to be taken into consideration to establish an employer-employee relationship would include inter-alia: 


(i) who appoints the workers; 

(ii) who pays the salary/remuneration; 

(iii) who has the authority to dismiss; 

(iv) who can take disciplinary action; 

(v) whether there is continuity of service; and 

(vi) extend of control and supervision i.e., whether there exists complete control and supervision.” 


22. Now after applying the principles as laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in this case, it appears that the 
sponsoring union/concerned workmen have not produced any documents regarding their appointment by the 
management of BCCL but their only contention is that since they are working in the coal transportation work for 
longer period, so their services could be regularized which is not sustainable in the eye of law without any documents. 
Further the sponsoring union/concerned workmen have not produced any wage slip/pay slip regarding payment of 
their salary/remuneration by the management of BCCL. Moreover it is the case of the management that they had 
allotted the contract work to transport contractors for transportation of coal from different sources of Block-II Area to 
the Railway siding, so they are not paying any wage to any of the concerned workmen. Further there is no evidence 
raised by the sponsoring union or the management regarding authority to dismiss or to take disciplinary action against 
the concerned workmen. Now, coming to the continuity of service, it appears that sponsoring union has been 
consistent in their evidence that they were working for last twenty years but they have not produced any chit of paper 
to show their engagement from the year 995 to till now. They have only produced the photo copy of passbook of 
CMPF which does not seems to be reliable, so the sponsoring union/workmen has failed to establish the continuity of 
service under the management of Block-II Area of M/s. BCCL. 


23. The last point of consideration is control and supervision of the concerned workmen, On this point the sponsoring 
union/workman has tried to establish that their services were controlled and supervised by the management of BCCL 
but no such documents has been produced or filed by the union to show that the services of these workmen were 


[भाग वा--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 3, 2025/ज्येष्ठ 0, 947 3669 


under the control or supervision of the management of BCCL. However the management has been categorical in its 
statement that the work order has been awarded to the different transport contractors for transportation of coal from 
colliery depot to railway siding and the concerned workmen were not under the control and supervision of the 
management of BCCL. 


24. Now the Hon’ble Supreme Court in an another case Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd. Vs. Mahendra Prasad Jakhmola 
and Others, the Hon’ble Supreme Court has been pleased to hold that “After having assigned the workmen by the 
contractor to the principal employer, on the basis direction by the principal employer to the workmen regarding 
performing of assigned job, it cannot be said that workmen were under the administrative control and supervision of 
the principal employer since there was no appointment letter, provident fund or wage slip from principal employer — 
Hence, contract between principal employer and contractor is not sham.” 


25. In view of above discussion and in view of decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court it is quite apparent that the 
contract order of the management of BCCL to the different contractors are not sham and camouflage as raised by the 
workmen/union. 


26.After considering all the facts and circumstances of the case and after analyzing all the evidences available on the 
record the Tribunal finds and holds that the demand of Bihar Colliery Kamgar Union, Dhanbad for regularization of 
services of 22 workmen by the management of Block-II Area of M/s. BCCL is not justified and consequently all the 
concerned 22 workmen are not entitled to any relief in this case. 


This is the Award of this Tribunal. 


DINESH KUMARSINGH,Presiding Officer

AWARD 


By Order No.L-2002/494/999-(C-I) dated 07.03.2000, the Central Government in theMinistry of Labour 
has, in exercise of the powers conferred by clause (d) of sub-section (l) and sub section (2A) of Section !0 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 947, referred the following disputes for adjudication to this Tribunal: 


SCHEDULE 


“Whether deployment of 02 Munshis by the Mgt. of CCL through contractors on work of regular 
and permanent nature viz. recording of transportation movement of coal etc. instead of giving them 
regular appointment in CCL is just, proper and legal? 


2. Whether action of M/s. Ranguta Projects Ltd. and other contractors of M/s. CCL in denying employment ad 
wages to these workmen w.e.f. 23.4.98 is just and fair? If not, what directions are necessary in this regard?”
