2. At the outset it is required to mention here that this Tribunal has answered the reference infavour of 02 workmen 
for payment of compensation of Rs. 75,000/-fo rthose workers who died or crossed the age of superannuation and 
their regularization who were less than fifty years of age under the management of M/s. CCL vide Award dated 
28.08.2043. 

3.The management of M/s. CCL has preferred writ petition before the Hon’ble Jharkhand High Court, Ranchi against 
the Award passed by this Tribunal and the Hon’ble Jharkhand High Court has been pleased to set aside the Award 
vide W.P.(L) No. 4499 of 205 dated 02.2.2024 and the matter is remitted back to this Tribunal for passing fresh 
Award. 

4. After receipt of the order of the Hon’ble Jharkhand High Court on 02.2.2024 the case was restored to the 
original file 

5. The case of the Union Bihar Colliery Kamgar Union as per its written statement is as follows:- 


That Sri Hiralal Bedia and other concerned workmen had been working as Munshies at Gidi Washery of M/s. 
Central Coalfields Limited since long and continuously in the permanent nature of job. All the concerned workmen 
had been working for more than 240 days in each calendar year and they had been performing the permanent nature of 
job under the management of Gidi Washery with direct control and supervision of the management. All the concerned 
workmen were doing the jobs of Munshies and rendering services of Gidi Washery management but the management 
had devised a camouflage system of exploiting the workmen in the name of alleged intermediary. The concerned 
workmen were not been paid wages as being paid to the permanent workmen. The alleged intermediaries were 
changing but the workmen were continuing their job for the benefits of the management of Gidi Washery. The 
disbursement of wages through alleged intermediary are nothing but legal camouflage. The management had entered 
into conciliation proceeding and had agreed to regularize all the concerned workmen who were performing the job of 
Munshies and connected with transportation of coal but subsequently the management refused to regularize them as 
they were the members of Bihar Colliery Kamgar Union. The intermediaries were neither possessing any licence nor 
the management was possessing registration certificate as per law, so all the concerned workmen were the employees 
of the management. The union had earlier raised the dispute before the management and the same was referred to 
CGIT No.2, Dhanbad which was registered as Ref. Case No. 40/9] and I50/9] but the Tribunal passed an award on 
November, !993 holding the concerned workmen not entitled for regularization on the ground that they had not put in 
240 days attendance in each calendar year. In the meantime the concerned workmen were working but the 
management was not paying them wages directly or through intermediaries since April’ 998 and subsequently 
stopped them from service after that the union raised an industrial dispute before ALC and RLC (C), Dhanbad wherein 
decided to reinstate the concerned workmen. The deployment of !02 Munshies (workmen) by the management of 
CCL through contractors on work of regular and permanent nature are not proper and legal, so the action of the 
management was illegal and arbitrary. 


A prayer has been made for passing an award in favour of the workmen with the direction to the management 
to pay their wages or reinstatement with effect from 23.4.998 with all arrear of wages and other attendant benefits. 


6. The case of the management Central Coal Field Limited as per its written statement is as follows:- 


That the union has got no locus standi to raise the industrial dispute on behalf of the person concerned . The 
Central Government Industrial Tribunal No.2, Dhanbad vide its Award dated — November, 993 in Ref. Case 
No. 40/99 and 50/I99 had held that the persons concerned are not entitled for regularization in the services of 
C.C.L. management and the same is hit by the Principles of resjudicata. There is no employer-employees relationship 
between the management of M/s. CCL and the concerned workmen. In the year !996 there was trouble at Giddi 
Washery regarding payment of wages of Munshies deployed by the transport contractors and settlement was arrived 


[भाग ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 3, 2025/ज्येष्ठ 0, 947 3673 


between the management and transport contractors. The management of CCL had awarded contract for transportation 
of coal to the various contractors and the contractors deputed their own men for transportation of coal and the 
workmen concerned were recruited by the transport contractors. The management had no concern with the workmen 
of the contractors engaged on such jobs as they were purely contractors’ workers selected and paid waged by them. 
The management had not issued any notification under the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition Act, 970) 
abolishing the contract system in transportation of coal from Colliery/Washery/Depo to Railway Siding. 


A prayer has been made to hold that the concerned workmen are not entitled for any relief. 
7. The case of the management of M/s. Rungta Projects Ltd. as per its written statement is as follows: - 


That this reference is not maintainable because of non-joinder of parties. The Rungta Project Limited had 
engaged only 22 Munshies at Gidi Washery of C.C.L. upto April 998 and those Munshies were under its direct 
control and supervision and were not under the management of C.C.L. The contract of transportation of coking coal at 
Giddi Washery expired on 237 April 998 as a result 22 Munshies engaged earlier by it at Giddi Washery were not 
engaged. Further the termination of services of the 22 Munshies and payment of due wages to them were done through 
written communication on record. There was no victimization of the concerned workmen at the hands of 
intermediaries rather the concerned workmen had resorted violence and physical obstruction, damage to its 
equipments. The contract job from C.C.L. to R.P.L was for a limited period which expired on 23™ April 998 and 
services of 22 Munshies engaged by Giddi Washery were terminated and they were paid their due wages till that date. 


A prayer has been made to answer the reference in favour of the management. 


8. The union has filed rejoinder to the written statement of the management of C.C.L. and the management of 
Rungta Project Limited, denying all the averments made in their written statements. 


9. The sponsoring union has examined two witnesses they are WW-l, Hiralal Sharma and ४७-२2, 
Ram Bilas Prasad. 


The sponsoring union has not proved and exhibited any documents in support of its case. 
0. The management has examined only one witness. He is MW-I, Surajit Mallick. 
The management has not proved and exhibited any documents in support of its case. 
FINDINGS 


ll. At the outset of discussion the Tribunal thinks it proper to discuss first of all oral evidence of both the 
parties. 


The WW-|, Hiralal Sharma has deposed that he is one of the concerned workmen of this case and he knows all the 
others workmen of this case. He has also deposed that he has been deposing on behalf of all the concerned workmen. 
He has also stated that he and other workmen were working as Munshies of Giddi Washery since long continuously to 
the satisfaction of the management. He has also deposed that the post of Munshies was a permanent nature of job and 
they had been under the direct control and supervision of the management. He has also deposed that they had been 
rendering services and producing goods for the management of Giddi Washery. He has further deposed that the coal 
from different colliery of M/s. C.C.Ltd. was transported to Giddi Washery and the un-loading of coal and transporting 
the same is also connected with the production of the washery. He has further stated that the management had 
regularized the services of similarly situated Munshies who were the members of R.C.M.S. Union by entering into a 
conciliation settlement dated 9.4.982 and they had also represented before the management for their regularization 
but the management turned down their request. He has also stated that his case was referred to CGIT No.2, Dhanbad 
being read as Ref. Case No. l40/9] and 50/9! in which the Tribunal passed an award holding that they were not 
entitled for regularization only on the ground of not putting 240 days attendance in a year. He has further stated that 
after getting hold of documents to prove 240 days attendance in a year they had raised the present dispute and they had 
filed attendance register for the year !997. He has not proved the signature on the attendance register and subsequently 
he has not identified the same. He has also deposed that they had also called for attendance register for the year 984 
to till date but the management had neither produced the same nor had given any explanation for non-production of the 
same. He has further deposed that they had worked for 240 days in each calendar year and they were actually the 
employee of the management of C.C.L., so they are entitled for regularization. 


In the cross-examination he has deposed that he knew Rungta Brothers who was transporting contractor and 
he was not appointed by Rungta Brothers. He has also deposed that he has not worked under Rungta Contractor. He 
has also deposed that he had got no appointment letter from CCL and CCL had not issued him any Identity Card. He 
has also deposed that they had filed Ref. Case No. 40-9 before CGIT No.2, Dhanbad in which award was passed 
against them which was not challenged. 


2. The WW-2, Bilas Prasad has deposed that he is one of the concerned workmen and he knows all other 
concerned workmen of this case. He has further deposed that he has been deposing on behalf of all the workmen and 
they were working as Munshi continuously since !984-85 which was a permanent nature of job under the direct 


3674 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 3], 2025/JY AISTHA 0, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


control and supervision of management. He has also deposed that they had been working as Munshies on behalf of 
Giddi Washery and had been looking after smooth functioning of transportation of coal from different colliery. He has 
also stated that they had filed Ref. Case No. 40/9! and 50/9] and in both the cases awards were passed denying their 
regularization on the ground that they had not completed 240 days of attendance in a year. He has deposed that 
attendance register had been filed which had been marked as Exhibit W-! and accordingly they put more than 240 
days attendance in each calendar year. He has further deposed that they had been performing the job of Munshies 
which is permanent nature of job as per NCWA but the management instead of giving them regular appointment 
illegally called them employees of the alleged contractor. 


In the cross-examination he has deposed that he has not filed any document to show that he has been 
appointed as Munshi by CCL management and he had not gone to High Court against the Award of the CGIT No.2, 
Dhanbad. He has also deposed that he has got no paper to show that he had been paid by CCL management. He has 
also deposed that they were working through contractor of the work of the management. 


3. The MW-I, Surajit Mallick has deposed that he has deposed that he is Sr. Manager (Personnel) of Kedla 
Washery of M/s. CCL and he is conversant with this case. He has deposed that there has been no employer and 
employee relationship between the management of M/s. CCL and the concerned workmen. He has also deposed that 
the management of M/s. CCL had awarded contract for transportation of coal to the various contractors and 
contractors used to depute their own men for transporation of coal and management has no concern with the workmen 
of the contractors engaged on such jobs. He has also deposed that the contractors had selected, paid and controlled the 
concerned workmen and there is no relationship of employer and employee between the management of CCL and the 
concerned workmen. 


In the cross-examination he has deposed that he has no knowledge about the Giddi Washery and he has no 
any idea whether any transport contractor was engaged there. He has also deposed that as per NCWA there was a post 
having designation of Munshi. He has further deposed that he could not say whether there is any workmen and 
employer relationship between the parties of this case. 


4. Now, the Tribunal will analyze the oral evidence adduced by both the parties in the lights of pleadings of 
both the parties. 


49% It is the case of the union that there were !02 workmen working as Munshies in the different Washery of M/s. 
Central Coal Field Limited since long and they have performed their duties for 240 days in a calendar year. However, 
the management has categorically denied the averments of the union that the concerned workmen were working under 
the management of CCL. 


6. It is relevant to mention here that in this case the concerned workmen has not proved and exhibited any 
documents though in the affidavit evidence of WW-| it is mentioned that they have filed attendance register of the 
year |997 but the witness had not identified the signature of any person on it and consequently it has not been marked 
as Exhibit. However the WW-2 in his evidence has stated that attendance register has been filed and same has been 
marked as Exhibit-W-| but he has neither proved the attendance register nor identified the same, so the attendance 
register was not marked as Exhibit. 


The management has also not proved any documents in support of its case. 


7. Here in this case the sponsoring union or workmen have also not filed any documents to show that the 
concerned workmen had worked for 240 days in a calendar year. However, the workmen has produced document of 
attendance of the year 997, in which there is a list of 45 workmen but that document has not been proved or identified 
by the Sponsoring Union, so that list is not being taken into consideration. 


8. In this case the workmen has not produced any documents to show that all the workmen have been working under 
the management of CCL. Further both WW-I and WW-2 in their cross-examination have admitted that management 
of CCL had not issued any appointment letters to them. Further WW-I and WW-2 have also admitted that they have 
not received any Pay Slip issued by the management. 


9. It is relevant to mention here that the Ministry of Labour & Employment has referred the dispute of same 
and similar nature between the concerned workmen and the management of CCL before the CGIT No.2, Dhanbad in 
Ref. Case No. 40/9I and 50/9. Further the ४४५७४-] and WW-2 has admitted that in both the cases Awards have been 
passed against the union workmen on the ground that they had not completed attendance of 240 days in a 
calendar year. 


20. Now, in this case the concerned workmen have not brought into record any documents to show that they 
worked under the management of CCL since 984, so the evidence of WW-! and WW-2 on this point are not reliable. 


2). At this stage it is relevant to mention here that the decision of Hon’ble Supreme Court passed in Balwant 
Rai Saluja vs. Air India Ltd., (204) 9 SCC 407, in which the Hon’ble Supreme Court has been pleased to hold that 
the “relevant factors to be taken into consideration to establish an employer-employee relationship would include 
inter-alia: 


(i) who appoints the workers; 


[भाग [ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 3, 2025/ज्येष्ठ 0, 947 3675 


(ii) who pays the salary/remuneration; 

(iii) who has the authority to dismiss; 

(iv) who can take disciplinary action; 

(v) whether there is continuity of service; and 

(vi) extend of control and supervision i.e., whether there exists complete control and supervision.” 


22. Now after applying the principles as laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in this case, it appears that the 
sponsoring union/concerned workmen have not produced any documents regarding their appointment by the 
management of CCL but their only contention is that since they are working as Munshies work for longer period, so 
their services could be regularized which is not sustainable in the eye of law without any documents. 


Further the sponsoring union/concerned workmen have not produced any wage slip/pay slip regarding payment of 
their salary/remuneration by the management of CCL. Moreover it is the case of the management of CCL that 
management had awarded contract for transportation of coal to the various contractors and the contractors deputed 
their own men for transportation of coal and the workmen concerned were recruited by the transport contractors, so 
they are not paying any wage to any of the concerned workmen. 


Further there is no evidence raised by the sponsoring union or the management regarding authority to dismiss or to 
take disciplinary action against the concerned workmen. 


Now, coming to the continuity of service, it appears that sponsoring union has been consistent in their 
evidence that they were working since 984 but they have not produced any documents in this regard. However WW- 
l and WW- 2 in their evidence have mentioned about attendance register but they have not proved the said register as a 
result the said register was not marked, so the sponsoring union/workmen has failed to establish the continuity of 
service under the management of M/s. CCL. 


23. The last point of consideration is control and supervision of the concerned workmen, On this point the 
sponsoring union/workman has tried to establish that their services were controlled and supervised by the management 
of CCL but no such documents has been produced or filed by the union to show that the services of these workmen 
were under the control or supervision of the management of CCL. However the management has been categorical in 
its statement that the work order has been awarded to the different transport contractors for transportation of coal and 
contractors used to depute their own men for transportation of coal and the concerned workmen were not under the 
control and supervision of the management of CCL. 


24. Now the Hon’ble Supreme Court in an another case Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd. Vs. Mahendra Prasad 
Jakhmola and Others, the Hon’ble Supreme Court has been pleased to hold that “After having assigned the workmen 
by the contractor to the principal employer, on the basis direction by the principal employer to the workmen 
regarding performing of assigned job, it cannot be said that workmen were under the administrative control and 
supervision of the principal employer since there was no appointment letter, provident fund or wage slip from 
principal employer — Hence, contract between principal employer and contractor is not sham.” 


25. In view of above discussion and in view of decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court it is quite apparent that the 
contract order of the management of CCL to the different contractors are not sham and camouflage as raised by the 
workmen/union. 


26. In view of above discussions the Tribunal finds and holds that the management of Central Coal Field Limited 
in not giving regular appointment to all the concerned workmen is just proper and legal. 


2s Now the next point of consideration in this case is regarding denying of employment and wages to these 
workmen w.e.f. 23.4.98 by M/s. Rungta Project Limited and others contractor of M/s. CCL. 


28. In this regard it has been mentioned in a written statement filed by the M/s. Rungta Project Limited that they 
have engaged only 22 workmen on the basis of contract given by CCL for transportation of coal to Giddi Washery and 
its contract expired on April !998, so there is no question of giving further employment to the workmen. In this regard 
the WW-I and WW-2 has deposed nothing regarding their payment of wages from M/s. Rungta Projects Limited 
w.e.f. 23.4.98 and denying their employment. 


29. In absence of any evidence on this point the Tribunal finds and holds that the concerned workmen/union has 
failed to establish regarding non-payment of wages w.e.f. 23.4.98 and denying employment to the workmen by M/s. 
Rungta Project Limited of M/s. CCL. 


It is required to mention here that it is an admitted fact that Ministry of Labour & Employment had referred 
same and similar dispute between all the concerned workmen and the management of CCL vide Ref. Case No. 40/9 
and 50/9! in CGIT No.2, Dhanbad and both case were answered against the workmen but the workmen have not 
challenged the said award, so both the cases reached finality. 


30. After considering all the facts and circumstances of the case and after analyzing all the evidence available on 
the record, the Tribunal comes to the conclusion that all the !02 concerned workmen are not entitled for regularization 
of services under the management of CCL and they are also not entitled for payment of any wages by M/s. Rungta 


3676 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 3, 2025/JY AISTHA 0, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


Project Ltd. w.e.f. 23.4.98. Moreover all the 02 concerned workmen are not entitled for any relief. 
This is the Award of this Tribunal.

This case coming before me for final hearing in the presence of S/Sri K. Sadan Kumar, B. Amarendar Rao 
and G. Venkatesh, Advocates for the Petitioner/Workman and of Sri T. Ravinder Singh, Standing Counsel for the 


Respondent/Management; and having been heard and having stood over for consideration till this day, the Tribunal 
delivered the following:- 


AWARD 


This petition is filed U/Sec.2-A (2) of ID. Act praying to set aside the dismissal order dt.24..999 passed 
by the Respondent and direct the Respondents’ Company to reinstate the petitioner into service with continuity of 
service, together with all attendant benefits and full back wages. 


2. It is submitted that the Hon’ble High Court vide its Common Order dt.07.06.2024 in W.P.Nos.l976/2005 and 
23909/2005 has remanded back the matter to this Tribunal for fresh adjudication and to give findings on the grounds 
sought to be raised by both the parties, including opportunity of personal hearing and strict verification of documents 
and pass appropriate orders in accordance with law, within six months from the date of receipt of a copy of this order. 


[भाग ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 3, 2025/ज्येष्ठ 0, 947 3677 


As per the above orders of the Hon'ble High Court, this Tribunal issued notices and both parties have appeared before 
this Tribunal and adduced their evidence and rival arguments. 


3. The brief averments of the petition are as follows: 


3(a). The petitioner was appointed as Female General Mazdoor in place of her husband who was found medical- 
unfit and she worked for (0) years without any remarks. But from 998, she suffered with ill-health, Hypertension 
and Jaundice, for which she became very weak and suffered with neuro problem. She was unable to move, she was 
under sick w.e.f., 25.4.998 and sent copy of private sick certificate but it was not accepted, treated as absent and 
issued charge sheet dt.07.02.999, framing following charge: 


Absent for duty from 26.04.998 to 05.02.999, amounts misconduct under Company's Standing Order 25(3) 
which read as: “Absence from duty without sanctioned leave or cause or overstaying beyond sanctioned leave”. 


The petitioner suffered with Hypertension and Infective Hepatitis decease from !998 and was admitted in the 
Company Hospital on 2.2.999. She was in the Hospital for (5) days and discharged on 6.02.999 with fit 
certificate. That the doctors have observed the sickness of last one year, arranged investigations, given medicines and 
advised to report for duty. When reported for duty, she was not taken to duty due to weakness and advised to come 
after recovery from ill-health. 


3(b). The petitioner is illiterate, believed the Colliery Manager and taken treatment by staying at her residence. She 
has not received any enquiry letter and due to illiteracy she had not seen the paper publication. But, the Enquiry 
Officer conducted exparte enquiry against the principles of natural justice. The respondent has not communicated 
enquiry report, not call-for objections/comments on the enquiry report, not issued the Show Cause notice of dismissal 
from service and directly dismissed her from service. She preferred an appeal to the Director, (PAW) and to the 
Chairman & Managing Director but there is no response. The respondent dismissed her from service vide Proc. 
dt.24..999, due to which she is suffering for food, poverty and unable to maintain her family. She mentally 
suffered and applied for Voluntary retirement on 26.0.999 i.e., prior to dismissal from service which was not agreed 
and she was dismissed from service. The petitioner was dismissed from the service, which attracts Sec.2(A) (2) of 
I.D.Act, hence this petition is maintainable. The petitioner is a poor woman, not defrauded any revenues and the 
capital punishment of dismissal from the service is shockingly disproportionate. Hence, she prays to set aside the 
dismissal from service proceedings and direct the respondent to reinstate her into service with continuity of service, 
together with all attendant benefits and full back wages. 


4. On the other side, the Respondent’s/Company have submitted rejoinder by admitting the employment of the 
Petitioner/Workman with the Respondent’s/Company and inter-alia contended that the respondent company is a Govt. 
Company incorporated under the provisions of Companies Act, !956 for carrying out the business of winning and 
selling the coal. Since the coal mining industry is a central subject, appropriate Government is Central Government. 
Further, Central Government Industrial Tribunal was established at Hyderabad from 29.2.2000 for adjudication of 
industrial disputes and the petitioner ought to have approached the said tribunal for the redressal of grievance, if any. 
But, the petitioner conveniently avoided to file her petition before the tribunal established by the Central Government 
and hence, this petition is not maintainable under law and the same may be dismissed in limini. 


4(a). The petitioner was appointed as Temporary General Mazdoor (sweeper) under dependant employment scheme 
on 26.08.990. As she remained absent from 26.04.998 to 05.02.999 without prior permission or sanctioned leave, 
she was issued with charge sheet dt.07.02.999 under clause ।२०.25(3|) of company's approved standing orders. She 
did not submit any private sick certificate for the period she was absent for duty at any point of time and if she was ill, 
she would have reported at company’s hospital for necessary treatment and availed sick leave. The respondent’s 
company is maintaining super specialty hospitals in all areas to cater the health and medical needs of its employees at 
free of cost. The petitioner is fully aware of the same and did not avail the facility. She received charge sheet on 
09.02.999, took treatment in the company hospital as an after-thought and did not submit any explanation. As the 
petitioner was not attending for her duties, notice regarding date of enquiry was sent through registered post with ack. 
due to her permanent address. But the same was returned un-served as she was not available at that address. The 
enquiry notice was published in Vartha Telugu daily news paper on 28.7.!999 advising her to attend for enquiry on 
09.08.999. As she failed to attend the enquiry, exparte enquiry was conducted on 09.08.[999. Further, a copy of 
enquiry proceedings and report were served to petitioner on 7.0.999 with an advice to make any representation 
against the findings of the enquiry report. 


4(b). Further, the petitioner vide letter dt.26.0.999 requested the company to allow her for voluntary retirement and 
to put her son in her place as her dependant as she was unable to continue the job due to her illness. As her 
representation is not tenable under the standing orders of the respondent company and as she worked for 44-days in 
998 and 84-days in 999 and as there are no extenuating circumstances warranting less punishment than that of 
dismissal, her services were dismissed vide order dt.24..999 with effect from 25..999. She never submitted any 
appeal to the concerned and as the charge leveled against her was proved; her representation for voluntary retirement 
was not considered. If the employees are habitually abstain/abscond from their duties, planned production targets will 
not be achieved resulting in huge losses to the respondent’s company. Therefore, the respondent prayed to dismiss the 
petition without granting any relief to the petitioner. 


3678 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 3], 2025/JY AISTHA 0, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 
5. In support of the claim of the Petitioner/Workman, he got marked Ex.W-| to Ex.W-4 and on the other side 
for the Respondents/Corporation Ex.M-| to Ex.M-I] were marked. 


6. Heard, the learned counsel for Petitioner/Workman as well as Junior Law Officer for the 
Respondents/Corporation, besides written arguments on both sides. 


7. Now the points for consideration are:- 


L. Whether this Industrial Dispute is maintainable before this Tribunal or not? 

2. Whether the domestic enquiry conducted by the respondents is held valid or not? 

3. Whether the charge leveled against the petitioner is proved basing on evidence or not? 

4. Whether the dismissal order 4/.24.॥7.॥999 is liable to be set aside, if so, the petitioner is entitled to 


reinstatement with continuity of service with all attendant benefits and full back wages? 
5. Tf not to what relief is the worker entitled to? 


8. From the pleadings of the Petitioner/Workman and Respondents’ Company, these are the admitted facts that the 
petitioner worked as Temporary General Mazdoor (sweeper) in the respondent’s company and he was dismissed from 
service. Now coming to the documentary evidence on both sides, on behalf of the Respondents’/Company, Ex.M-| to 
Ex.M-] were marked, wherein, Ex.M-! is Charge Sheet dt.07.02.999 which was acknowledged by the petitioner on 
09.02.999. Ex.M-2 is the letter appointing one Sri M.Rajendra Kumar as Enquiry Officer to conducting enquiry. 
Ex.M-3 is Enquiry Notice issued to the petitioner and Ex.M-4 is Undelivered postal cover with ack. Ex.M-5 is 
Vaartha Telugu Daily News Paper publication of enquiry notice. Ex.M-6 is Enquiry proceedings and Ex.M-7 is 
Enquiry report dt.l2.08.999. Ex.M-8 is Show Cause notice dt.!3.0.999 wherein it shows that a copy of enquiry 
report was sent to the petitioner requiring her to submit her representation; and Ack., of petitioner dt.l7.0.999. 
Ex.M-9 is Representation of petitioner dt.26.0.!999 wherein it shows that she is unable to continue her job and her 
son is interested to work in the Company; and she requested to allow her for voluntary retirement. Ex.M-0 is 
Dismissal Order dt.24..999 issued to the petitioner and Ex.M-I is Office Memo removing her name from the 
rolls of the company. On the other side, the petitioner got marked Ex.W-| to Ex.W-4 on her behalf, wherein, 7. ४४-। 
is Medical certificate dt.05.02.999. Ex.W-2 is Discharge card dt.6.02.999, wherein it shows that petitioner is “Fit 
for Duty”. Ex.W-3 is Copy of quarter allotment letter and Ex.W-4 is Dismissal Order (photo copy). The above 
documents of both sides are not in much dispute by either side. 


9. Here, the learned counsel for the respondents’-company has strenuously put forth and set forth that since the coal 
mining industry is a central subject, the Appropriate Government, which established Central Govt. Industrial Tribunal 
at Hyderabad for adjudication of Industrial Disputes and the Petitioner ought to have approached the said Tribunal for 
the redressal of grievance, if any. But, the Petitioner conveniently avoided filing her petition before the Tribunal 
established by the Central Government and hence this I.D is not maintainable before this Tribunal and and the same is 
liable to be dismissed on this ground alone. 


9(a). The learned counsel for the respondent’s-company further strenuously put forth and set forth that the petitioner 
was appointed as Temporary General Mazdoor (sweeper) under dependant employment scheme on 26.08.!990 and 
she remained absent to her duties from 26.04.998 to 05.02.999 without any prior permission or sanctioned leave. 
She was issued with charge sheet dt.07.02.999, she received the same on 09.02.999 and did not submit any 
explanation. She took treatment in the company hospital as an after-thought and as she was not attending for her 
duties, enquiry notice was sent through RPAD to her permanent address. But as the same was returned un-served, 
enquiry notice was published in Vaartha Telugu daily news paper on 28.7.999 advising her to attend for enquiry on 
09.08.999. But, she failed to attend the enquiry and hence, exparte enquiry was conducted on 09.08.999. Further, a 
copy of enquiry proceedings and report were served to petitioner on !7.0.999 with an advice to make any 
representation against the findings of the enquiry report. She submitted letter dt.26.0.999 requesting the company to 
allow her for voluntary retirement and to put her son in her place as her dependant as she was unable to continue the 
job, which is not tenable under the company’s standing orders. Further, she worked for 44-days during 998 and 84- 
days during 999 and as there are no extenuating circumstances, her services were dismissed vide order 
dt.24..999, which is justified. She never submitted any appeal to the concerned authorities of the company. Hence, 
he prayed to dismiss the petition, without granting any relief to the petitioner. 


0. Per contra, on the point of jurisdiction, the learned counsel for the Petitioner has put forth and set forth that as per 
the Division Bench Judgment of the Hon’ble High Court reported in 997 (IH) LLJ (Supp.) ll, Between: U. 
Chinnappa Vs. Cotton Corporation of India, this Tribunal has jurisdiction over Singareni Collieries Company Ltd., to 
entertain the Industrial Dispute raised by the petitioner though the appropriate Govt. is Central Govt., The petitioner 
need not raise the Industrial Dispute compulsorily before the Central Govt. Industrial Tribunal, Hyderabad alone, as 
contended by the respondents’ company. Hence, this I.D petition filed by the petitioner is well maintainable before 
this Tribunal for adjudication of the dispute on merits. 


0(a). The learned counsel for the Petitioner further put forth and set forth that the Petitioner was appointed was 


[भाग ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 3, 2025/ज्येष्ठ 0, 947 3679 


appointed during the year 990 as a dependant in place of his husband and served the respondents’ company more 
than 8-years. From the year 998, she suffered with ill-health, Hypertension and Jaundice, for which she became very 
weak and suffered with neuro problem. She was unable to move, she was under sick w.e.f., 25.4.998. Further, she 
was admitted in the Company Hospital on 2.2.999, treated for (5) days and was discharged on 6.02.999 with fit 
certificate. She has not received any enquiry letter and due to illiteracy she had not seen the paper publication. But, 
the Enquiry Officer conducted exparte enquiry and was dismissed her from service unjustly vide Proc. dt.24..999, 
due to which she is suffering for food, poverty and unable to maintain her family. She applied for Voluntary 
retirement on 26.0.999 i.e., prior to dismissal from service which was not agreed and she was dismissed from 
service, which is shockingly disproportionate. Further, as the petitioner attained retirement age, he prays to set aside 
the dismissal order and direct the respondent’s company to treat the petitioner as if she was retired from service with 
continuity of service, together with all attendant benefits and full back wages. 


ll. Admittedly, the Hon’ble High Court passed Common Order dt.07.06.2024 in W.P.Nos.l976/2005 and 
23909/2005 remanded back the matter to this Tribunal for fresh adjudication in accordance with law. As per the 
orders of the Hon'ble High Court, on issuing notices, both parties have appeared before this Tribunal and they have 
put forth and set forth their respective arguments. 


POINT No. I: 


2. Here, on the point of territorial jurisdiction of this Tribunal, it is settled Law that as per the Division Bench 
Judgment of the Hon’ble High Court reported in 997 (IID) LLJ (Supp.) , Between: U. Chinnappa Vs. Cotton 
Corporation of India, this Tribunal has got every jurisdiction to entertain the Industrial Dispute raised by the 
petitioner/workman who was an employee of Singareni Collieries Company Ltd., Even though, the Central Govt. is 
appropriate Govt., for the respondents’-Company, the petitioner need not compulsorily raise the Industrial Dispute 
before the Central Govt. Industrial Tribunal, Hyderabad, as contended by the respondents’ company; and he can file 
this I.D. case before this Tribunal as well. Hence, the contentions of the respondents’-company on the point of 
jurisdiction of this Tribunal are not sustainable under Law. Accordingly, it is answered in favour of the petitioner and 
against the respondents’ Singareni Collieries Company Limited. 


POINT No. 2: 


3. Further, in this matter, initially the petitioner/workman denied the validity and legality of the enquiry report. 
But on 27.02.2025, the learned counsel for petitioner filed Memo U/Sec. l-A of I.D.Act by accepting the procedure 
of domestic enquiry. Now the next question is whether the misconduct is proved in the facts of the case and the 
findings are not perverse. So, this Tribunal is to re-appreciate the evidence and come to its own conclusion with 
regard to finding guilty or not based on evidence. Accordingly, the Point No.| is answered. 


POINT No. 3 & 4: 


4. In view of the pleadings of the Petitioner/Workman as well as Respondents/corporation as well as in view of the 
rival arguments of their respective counsel now this Court will go into the evidence on record. Admittedly, the 
petitioner was dismissed from service by Proc. dt.24.l.!999 wherein it is alleged that the petitioner was absent from 
duty without sanctioned leave or sufficient cause from the year 998. From a perusal of the record, it shows that 
Charge Sheet dt.07.02.!999 was issued to the petitioner, which is marked as Ex.M-]. It is evident from the charge 
sheet that the petitioner absented to her duties from 26.04.998 to 05.02.999 without any sanctioned leave or 
sufficient cause, which amounts to misconduct under company’s standing order 25(3l). The petitioner had 
acknowledged the charge sheet on 09.02.999 but she did not choose to submit any explanation. As the enquiry notice 
dt.22.06.999 which is marked as Ex.M-3 was returned un-served under Ex.M-4, notice was enquiry was published in 
the News Paper, which is marked as Ex.M-4. Enquiry Proceedings are marked as Ex.M-6, wherein it shows that the 
petitioner was not present for the enquiry and exparte enquiry was conducted. Further, a perusal of Ex.M-6 
proceedings of enquiry shows that Sri M.Shankaraiah, Office Superintendent and Md.Ziaur Rahman, Pay sheet clerk 
were examined by the enquiry officer. Further, Sri S.Chandraiah, Peon deposed that he called the petitioner 3-times 
loudly to appear for enquiry, but no response was found by him and he informed the same to the Enquiry Officer. 
Further, Sri M.Shankaraiah, Office Superintendent and Sri Md.Ziaur Rahman, pay sheet clerk have categorically 
deposed in support of the charge framed against the petitioner and stated that the petitioner remained absent for duty 
from 26.04.998 to 05.02.999. Further it is borne on record that the petitioner did not give any information to the 
respondent’s office about her absence to duty and the concerned pay sheets and Form “C” Registers from April 998 
to February 999 were produced by the witnesses during enquiry. It is evident that the petitioner did not choose 
appear before the Enquiry Officer and failed to participate in the enquiry, for the reasons best known to her. 


5. Apart from the above, the Enquiry Report dt.2.08.999 is marked as Ex.M-7 wherein it shows that the Enquiry 
Officer held and concluded that the charge was proved against the petitioner basing on the statements and records 
produced during enquiry; and the petitioner Smt. Mandigam Mallamma is found guilty of misconduct under the 
Company’s Standing Order No.25(3). Further, the discharge summary dt.6.02.999 is marked as Ex.W-2 wherein it 
shows that the petitioner was admitted on 2.02.!999 and she was discharged on !6.02.999 by making endorsement 
as “Fit for Duty”. This document clearly shows that the petitioner/ workman took treatment after issuing charge sheet 
under Ex.M-|. Further, it is clear that the petitioner has not attended to duties during the charge sheet period from 
26.04.998 to 05.02.999, not submitted any explanation, she did not participate in the enquiry and the charge was 


3680 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 3], 2025/JY AISTHA 0, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


proved against the petitioner, basing on record. Therefore, it can be said that the respondent’s-company has no axe to 
grind against the petitioner. Hence, this Tribunal has no hesitation to hold that the charge leveled against the 
petitioner/ workman is proved and misconduct of the workman is established basing on the evidence and the findings 
of enquiry officer are not perverse. 


5(a). Apart from the above, the contention of the Petitioner is that she was appointed in the year 990 as a dependant 
of her deceased husband and worked for more than (8) years without any remarks. Further, the petitioner hails from a 
very poor family, she has got no other livelihood and facing untold financial problems, already attained 
superannuation age as she is aged about 62 years and prayed to consider the case U/Sec.ll-A of I.D. Act. These facts 
amounts to mitigating circumstances and in view of the above facts and circumstances of the case, this Tribunal is of 
the considered opinion that this is a fit case to exercise its discretion U/Sec.ll-A of I.D.Act and relying upon a 
decision of the Hon’ble High Court reported in 20I2 (!) ALD 220 (DB), wherein their lordships observed that: 


“The Industrial Disputes Act, /947 is a social welfare legislation, which required to be interpreted 
keeping in view the goals set out in the Preamble and Directive principles of State Policy in Part-IV of the 
Constitution. Merely because workman approached to Labour Court with delay, relief cannot be denied. No 
indication in the Act that delay extinguishes right conferred on the workmen under Industrial Law. The 
Labour Court is conferred with very wide discretion 9/8९९/7-4., The Industrial Court conferred with very 
wide discretion ७/१९८./7-4 of the Act for granting appropriate relief”. 


6. Further, this Tribunal relied upon the following judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court reported in: 


2020 (I)SCC 3]4 in the case of Charanjit Lamba Vs. Commanding Officer, Army Southern Command & 


others. 


Wherein their Lordships held that: Alternative lesser punishment of a compulsory retirement would be more 
reasonable and proportionate to the given circumstance of the case. However, in view of the charges proved 
against the conductor, it would not be appropriate to order for entire back wages, but, on the other hand, it 
would be modified to the effect that the legal heirs of the deceased workman would be entitled to receive the 
death-cum-retirement benefits, in the ends of justice. 


l6(a). Apart from the above, their Lordships of the Hon’ble Gujarat High Court in a case rendered on 04.05.994, 
Between: Management of Glaxo India Ltd., Vs. State of Assam and 3 others categorically observed that “a Labour 
Court is required to settle a dispute according to the principles of natural justice, equity and good conscience and 
law without attaching undue importance to legal technicalities”. 


7. This Tribunal has perused, analyzed and meditated upon the case at hand, the case laws and principles of law 
referred above. In view of the above facts and circumstances and keeping in view of the principle “temper justice with 
mercy” and to meet the ends of justice, this Tribunal is of the opinion that the punishment of dismissal imposed on the 
petitioner is disproportionate and shocks the conscience of this Tribunal and hence, it deserves to be modified 
appropriately. If we come to quantum of punishment it is settled law that the discretion of which can be exercised 
Under Sec.li-A is available only on the existence of certain factors like punishment being disproportionate to the 
gravity of misconduct so as to shock the conscience of the Court, or the existence of any mitigating circumstances 
which require the reduction of the punishment, or the past conduct of the workman which may persuade the Labour 
Court to reduce the punishment. In this case, the petitioner rendered more than (8) years service in the respondent’s 
company. Therefore, this Tribunal is of the considered opinion that the extreme punishment of dismissal from service 
imposed on the petitioner vide Proc. dt.24.!.999 is not commensurate and shockingly disproportionate, and hence 
deserves to be modified appropriately to that of retirement from service with effect from 24..999 only. 
Consequently, the petitioner is entitled to receive the retirement benefits and pension benefits from the respondents’ 
company, as per eligibility which would meet the ends of justice. However, the petitioner is not entitled to any 
continuity of service, any back wages and any attendant benefits. Accordingly, the Point No.3 & 4 are answered. 


8. IN THE RESULT, the petition is partly allowed. The dismissal order vide Proc. dt.24..999 under 
Ex.M-0 is modified to that of retirement from service with effect from 24.!.999 only. The respondent’s company 
is directed to pay consequential retirement benefits and pension benefits to the petitioner, as per eligibility. However, 
the petitioner is not entitled to any continuity of service, any back wages and any attendant benefits. Copy of the 
Award be sent to the appropriate Government for publication. Both parties shall bear their own costs.

Judgment 


By means of order no. L-42-2/2/2007-IR(DU) dated 28.6.2007, the Central Government considered it 
desirable to refer the dispute for adjudication to the following effect: - 


“Whether the action of management of Powerloom Development & Export Promotion Council, Mumbai in 
not following the provisions of Section 25F, 25G, 25H of Industrial Dispute Act 7947, while terminating the 
services of their workman Sri Janardhan S.Naik w.e.f. 27.5.2006 is legal and justified? If not, to what relief 
the workman is entitled to?” 


In pursuance to the said reference the statement of claim was filed on behalf of workman/applicant before this 
Tribunal and a CGIT No.34 of 2007 was registered. 


In the statement of claim, the workman pleaded that he was engaged by the Management as Peon since 4..996 to 
26.5.2006 continuously without any break in services. All of sudden his services was terminated illegally 
w.e.f. 27.5.2006 without any reason. Sri J.N. Singh acting as Chairman Staff Committee of the Management being 
the Commissioner of Ministry of Textiles at Mumbai has been looking after and deciding the day to day affairs of the 
Management. The workman worked for a period of l0 years and last drawn consolidated salary was Rs,3,700/-. All 
of sudden the services of workman had been terminated illegally without assigning any reason and without following 
the procedure or principle of natural justice for the reason best known to the Management. The workman’s whole 
service with the Management is without any complaint, very clean and unblemished. The Management has violated 
the law and committed serious unfair labour practice. After working for long period of l0 years, the workman has 
been terminated. The workman being not well educated and being a Peon could not get any job till date. The 
workman is required to lookafter his ailing mother, who is 70 years old; accordingly, he reqeusted that claim petition 
be allowed. 


On behalf of respondent the reply was filed to the statement of claim filed by workman in which it has been pleaded 
as under:- 


- The workman was working as a Peon with the Management. However, he has not working continuously 
with the Management for the period of 0 years as claimed. His last consolidated salary was Rs. 3700/- 
per month. 


- It is not true that the service was terminated illegally and without any reason. He was appointed by the 
Memorandum of the Management dated 2!.2.2006 under Ref No.PDEXCIL/ TEMP.STAFF/ 323/2006/ 
2526 for a period of 89 days from 27.2.2006 to 26.5.2006 on salary of Rs.3700/- per month on specific 
terms and conditions purely on temporary basis. 


- The Management denies that the workman was working continuously for the period of l0 years as 
claimed. The management was engaging his services on temporary basis for the period of 89 days from 
time to time as per the recommendation of the staff committee giving him priority in the services as he 
was available for the job. 


[भाग वा--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 3, 2025/ज्येष्ठ 0, 947 3683 


- The workman was issued certificate by the management showing his continuity of service for l0 years 
with the management of his request to issue such certificate to get him better employment. 


- The management has paid his last salary at the time of discontinuation of his service since, he was on 
temporary basis from time to time. He was not entitled the statutory benefits as applicable to the 
permanent employee/workmen of the management and the same has been clearly stated in his 
appointment letters from time to time, issued to him on his appointment. 


- The workman was appointed by letter with effect from 27.2.2006 as a Peon for the period of 89 days on 
contract basis on a consolidated salary of Rs.3,700/- per month. His service was discontinued on the 
basis of terms of the contract after 26.5.2006. Therefore the management need not entertain any of his 
correspondence or claim as alleged. 


Accordingly, it has been reqeusted on behlf of respodnent that the presetn case may kindly be dismissed. 


Finding & conclusion: 


I have heard Sri Janardhan S. Naik, workman and Ms. Ragni Sharma on behalf of respondent and gone through the 
records. 


In the city of Mumbai there is an establishment known as Powerloom Development & Export Promotion Council 
(hereinafter referred to as ‘establishment’) and in the said establishment the claimant/workman Sri Janardhan S.Naik 
was engaged as Peon w.e.f. 4..996 on consolidated salary of Rs.3700/- per month and his services were 
retrenched/terminated on 26/5/2006. 


Moreover, the said fact is evident from perusal of material available on record i.e. letter dated 29.5.2006, written by 
the Executive Director, Powerloom Development & Export Promotion Council (not disputed by the respondent) the 
relevant contents of which are quoted below:- 


“This is to certify that Mr. Janardhan S.Naik was working with the PDEXCIL as Peon from 747 November, 
/996 to 26" of May 2006. 


During his tenure in the PDEXCIL he was found to be very sincere, hard working and showed interest, 
enthusiasm in all his work. His stint at the PDEXCIL was absolutely satisfactory. During his tenure in the 
PDEXCIL we found him hard working, punctual and sincere in his duties. 


We wish all the success to his future career.” 


Taking into consideration the above said admitted facts and section 25-F of Industrial Disputes Act !947 which reads 
as under:- 


“257, Conditions precedent to retrenchment of workmen: 


- No workman employed in any industry who has been in continuous service for not less than one year under 
an employer shall be retrenched by that employer until- 


(a) the workman has been given one month 5४ notice in writing indicating the reasons for retrenchment 
and the period of notice has expired, or the workman has been paid in lieu of such notice, wages for the 
period of the notice: 


(b) the workman has been paid, at the time of retrenchment, compensation which shall be equivalent to 
fifteen days ‘average pay for every completed year of continuous service] or any part thereof in excess of six 
months; and 


(c) notice in the prescribed manner is served on the appropriate Government [or such authority as may 


be specified by the appropriate Government by notification in the Official Gazette.” 


The first & foremost question is to be considered that whether the workman has worked continuously for 240 days in 
the preceding twelve months in a calendar year or not? 


The workman in support of his case filed the following documents which were not denied by the respondent: - 


i) Memorandum no.PDEXCIL/TEMP.STAFF/323/2005/3727 dated 8.3.2005 issued by the Executive 
Director, Powerloom Development & Export Promotion Council; 


ii) Memorandum no.PDEXCIL/TEMP.STAFF/323/2005/359 dated 9.5.2005 issued by the Executive 
Director, Powerloom Development & Export Promotion Council; 


iii) © Memorandum no.PDEXCIL/TEMP.STAFF/323/2005/352 dated 20.8.2005 issued by the Executive 
Director, Powerloom Development & Export Promotion Council; 


iv) Memorandum no.PDEXCIL/TEMP.STAFF/323/2005/2034 dated 22.!.2005 issued by the Executive 
Director, Powerloom Development & Export Promotion Council; 


3684 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 3], 2025/JY AISTHA 0, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


v) Memorandum no.PDEXCIL/TEMP.STAFF/323/2005/2526 dated 2.2.2006 issued by the Executive 
Director, Powerloom Development & Export Promotion Council; 


vi) Certificate dated 29.5.2006 issued by the Executive Director, Powerloom Development & Export 
Promotion Council. 


Moreover the above said documents have already been proved by the workman by means of evidence on affidavit 
dated 0.0.20 and on the basis of cross examination dated 7.!.202. Further the management in its ‘affidavit on 
evidence’ did not dispute or deny neither the experience certificate dated 29.5.2006 quoted hereinabove nor other 
documents filed by the workman mentioned above. In view of the said facts it is clearly established that workman has 
continuously worked for more than 240 days in the last preceding calendar year before retrenchment of his services 
on 27.5.2006. 


Once it is established on the basis of pleadings, filing documents and evidence on record, the workman had worked 
240 days in the preceding twelve months in a calendar year then now a question arises that what relief is to be granted 
to the workman. 


Answer to the said question finds place in the case of Assistant Engineer, Rajasthan State Agriculture Marketing 
Board, Sub-Division, Kota vs. Mohan Lal reported in (203) 74 SCC 543, wherein it has been held that the 
respondent was engaged as a Mistri on muster roll basis, whose services were terminated. The workman was neither 
given one month's notice nor one month's salary was given in lieu of that notice, prior to termination of his service 
and he was also not paid retrenchment compensation. The industrial dispute, which was referred to the Labour Court 
culminated with the award made by the Labour Court, holding that as the workman had completed more than 240 
days in a calendar year and his services were being terminated in violation of Section 25- F of the Industrial Dispute 
Act, 947, the workman was entitled to be reinstated with continuity in service. 


The Single Judge of the Hon’ble High Court set aside the award and the Division Bench reinstated the award passed 
by the Labour Court. The Hon'ble Supreme Court observed that the workman had worked for 286 days from 
0I..984 to 7.02.986 and though the service of the workman was terminated w.e.f. 8.02.986, the industrial 
dispute was raised by the workman after six years. The Supreme Court thus held that the judicial discretion exercised 
by the Labour Court was flawed and unsustainable, in view of the delay of six years in raising the industrial dispute. 
However, the Supreme Court held that the interest of justice would be sub-served, if in lieu of reinstatement, 
compensation @ Rs.! Lakh was paid to the workman. 


In the case of U.P. State Road Transport Corporation vs. Man Singh reported in 2006 (777) FLR 323(SC), the 
service of the respondent, who was appointed on temporary basis, was terminated. The industrial dispute referred to 
the Labour Court culminated with the termination of the workman being set aside, in view of Section 25-F of the 
Industrial Dispute Act, 947, not being complied with. However, the workman was granted only back wages. The 
Hon’ble Supreme Court, on considering the fact that there was nothing to show that the workman had been appointed 
in accordance with the Recruitment Rules for filling up a vacancy, in terms of Article 4 and 6 of the Constitution, 
besides the fact that the dispute was raised after l2 years, the Hon’ble Supreme Court held that the interest of justice 
would be sub-served, if the Corporation was made to pay a sum of Rs. 50,000/- to the workman. 


In the case of Nand Kumar vs. State of Bihar and others reported in (2074) 5 SCC 300, the Hon’ble Supreme Court 
considered the judgment of the Constitution Bench in the case of State of Karnataka vs. Uma Devi reported in (2006) 
4 SCC 4, where it had held that while directing the appointments, temporary or casual, be regularized or made 
permanent, the Courts are swayed by the fact that the concerned person had worked for some time. It is not as if the 
person who accepts an engagement either temporary or casual in nature, is not aware of the nature of his employment. 
He accepts the employment with eyes open. It may be true that he is not in a position to bargain since he might have 
been searching for some employment so as to eke out his livelihood and accepts whatever he gets. But on that ground 
alone, it would not be appropriate to jettison the constitutional scheme of appointment and to take the view that a 
person who has temporarily or casually got employed should be directed to be continued permanently. By doing so, it 
would be creating another mode of public appointment which is not permissible. (see also State of Orissa vs. Mamata 
Mohanty reported in (2077) 3 SCC 436), 


Further the Madhya Pradesh Hon’ble High Court in the case of Branch Manager, Central Bank of India Tilak 
Chowk Vidisha Versus Pradeep Kumar Sen reported in 2024 (787) FLR 809 held as under:- 


“22. The Supreme Court in the case of Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited Vs. Bhurumal, reported in (2074) 7 
SCC 7/7 has held as under: - 


"33. It is clear from the reading of the aforesaid judgments that the ordinary principle of grant of 
reinstatement with full back wages, when the termination is found to be illegal is not applied 
mechanically in all cases. While that may be a position where services of a regular/permanent 
workman are terminated illegally and/or mala fide and/or by way of victimisation, unfair labour 
practice, etc. However, when it comes to the case of termination of a daily-wage worker and where 
the termination is found illegal because of a procedural defect, namely, in violation of Section 25-F 
of the Industrial Disputes Act, this Court is consistent in taking the view that in such cases 


[भाग Il—ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 3, 2025/ज्येष्ठ 0, 947 3665 


reinstatement with back wages is not automatic and instead the workman should be given monetary 
compensation which will meet the ends of justice. Rationale for shifting in this direction is obvious." 


23. The Supreme Court in the case of Jayant Vasantrao Hiwarkar Vs. Anoop Ganpatrao Bobde and others 
reported in (2077)377 SCC 244 has upheld the grant of compensation in lieu of reinstatement as the 
respondent had merely worked for a period of one year. 


24. The Supreme Court in the case of Hari Nandan Prasad and another Vs. Employer I/R to Management of 
Food Corporation of India and another, reported in (2074) 7 SCC 790 has held as under: - 


7॥9, The following passages from the said judgment would reflect the earlier decisions of this Court 
on the question of reinstatement: (BSNL case, SCC pp. 7867-66, paras 29-30) 


"29. The learned counsel for the appellant referred to two judgments wherein this Court granted 
compensation instead of reinstatement. In BSNL 9. Man Singh, this Court has held that when the 
termination is set aside because of violation of Section 25-F of the Industrial Disputes Act, it is not 
necessary that relief of reinstatement be also given as a matter of right. In Incharge Officer v. 
Shankar Shetty, it was held that those cases where the workman had worked on daily-wage basis, 
and worked merely for a period of 240 days or 2 to 3 years and where the termination had taken 
place many years ago, the recent trend was to grant compensation in lieu of reinstatement. 


30. In this judgment of Shankar Shetty, this trend was reiterated by referring to various judgments, 
as is clear from the following discussion: (SCC pp. 7227-26, paras 2-4) 


2. Should an order of reinstatement automatically follow in a case where the engagement of a 
daily-wager has been brought to an end in violation of Section 25-F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
4947 (for short "the ID Act")?The course of the decisions of this Court in recent years has been 
uniform on the above question. 


3. In Jagbir Singh v. Haryana State Agriculture Mktg. Board, delivering the judgment of this Court, 
one of us (R.M. Lodha, J.) noticed some of the recent decisions of this Court, namely, U.P. State 
Brassware Corpn. Ltd. v.Uday Narain Pandey, Uttaranchal Forest Development Corpn. v. M.C. 
Joshi, State of M.P. v. Lalit Kumar Verma, M.P. Admn. v. Tribhuban, Sita Ram v. Moti Lal Nehru 
Farmers Training Institute, Jaipur Development Authority v. Ramsahai, GDA v. Ashok Kumar and 
Mahboob Deepak v. Nagar Panchayat, Gajraula and stated as follows: (Jagbir Singh case, SCC 
pp.330 & 335, paras 7 & /4) 


"7. It is true that the earlier view of this Court articulated in many decisions reflected the legal 
position that if the termination of an employee was found to be illegal, the relief of reinstatement 
with full back wages would ordinarily follow. However, in recent past, there has been a shift in the 
legal position and in a long line of cases, this Court has consistently taken the view that relief by 
way of reinstatement with back wages is not automatic and may be wholly inappropriate in a given 
fact situation even though the termination of an employee is in contravention of the prescribed 
procedure. Compensation instead of reinstatement has been held to meet the ends of justice. 


जर4ब, It would be, thus, seen that by a catena of decisions in recent time, this Court has clearly laid 
down that an order of retrenchment passed in violation of Section 25-F although may be set aside 
but an award of reinstatement should not, however, be automatically passed. The award of 
reinstatement with full back wages in a case where the workman has completed 240 days of work in 
a year preceding the date of termination, particularly, daily-wagers has not been found to be proper 
by this Court and instead compensation has been awarded.This Court has distinguished between a 
daily-wager who does not hold a post and a permanent employee." 


4. Jagbir Singh has been applied very recently in Telegraph Deptt. v. Santosh Kumar Seal, wherein 
this Court stated:(SCC p. 777, para 77) 


Il. In view of the aforesaid legal position and the fact that the workmen were engaged as daily- 
wagers about 25 years back and they worked hardly for 2 or 3 years, relief of reinstatement and 
back wages to them cannot be said to be justified and instead monetary compensation would 
subserve the ends of justice.'" 


24. We make it clear that reference to Umadevi, in the aforesaid discussion is in a situation where 
the dispute referred pertained to termination alone. Going by the principles carved out above, had 
it been a case where the issue is limited only to the validity of termination, Appellant I would not be 
entitled to reinstatement........... 7 


25. The Supreme Court in the case of O.P.Bhandari Vs. Indian Tourism Development Corporation Limited 
and others reported (7966) 4 SCC 337 has held as under :- 


3686 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 3], 2025/JY AISTHA 0, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


"6. Time is now ripe to turn to the next question as to whether it is obligatory to direct reinstatement 
when the concerned regulation is found to be void. In the sphere of employer-employee relations in 
public sector undertakings, to which Article 72 of the Constitution of India is attracted, it cannot be 
posited that reinstatement must invariably follow as a consequence of holding that an order of 
termination of service of an employee is void. No doubt in regard to "blue collar" workmen and 
"white collar"employees other than those belonging to the managerial or similar high level cadre, 
reinstatement would be a rule, and compensation in lieu thereof a rare exception. Insofar as the 
high level managerial cadre is concerned, the matter deserves to be viewed from an altogether 
different perspective -- a larger perspective which must take into account the demands of National 
Interest and the resultant compulsion to ensure the success of the public sector in its competitive co- 
existence with the private sector. The public sector can never fulfil its life aim or successfully vie 
with the private sector if it is not managed by capable and efficient personnel with unimpeachable 
integrity and the requisite vision, who enjoy the fullest confidence of the "policy-makers" of such 
undertakings. Then and then only can the public sector undertaking achieve the goals of (7) 
maximum production for the benefit of the community, (2) social justice for workers, consumers and 
the people, and (3) reasonable return on the public funds invested in the undertaking. 


7. It is in public interest that such undertakings or their Boards of Directors are not compelled and 
obliged to entrust their managements to personnel in whom, on reasonable grounds, they have no 
trust or faith and with whom they are in a bona fide manner unable to function harmoniously as a 
team working arm-in-arm with success in the aforesaid three-dimensional sense as their common 
goal. These factors have to be taken into account by the court at the time of passing the 
consequential order, for the court has full discretion in the matter of granting relief, and the court 
can sculpture the relief to suit the needs of the matter at hand. The court, if satisfied that ends of 
justice so demand, can certainly direct that the employer shall have the option not to reinstate 
provided the employer pays reasonable compensation as indicated by the court." 


A division Bench of Hon’ble Gujarat High Court in the case of Range Forest Officer Versus Virjibhai 
Ranchhodbhai & another reported in 2024 (82) FLR 79 has held as under:- 


6.4. The shift in law on this count was highlighted by the Supreme Court in Bhopal Vs. Santosh Kumar 
Seal ((2079) 6 SCC 773] relying on its own another decision in Jagbir Singh Vs. Haryana State Agriculture 
Marketing Board [(2009) ॥5 SCC 327], observing that the relief of payment of lump-sum compensation 
could be a proper relief in a given set of facts and circumstances. 


"In the last few years it has been consistently held by this Court that relief by way of reinstatement 
with back wages is not automatic even if termination of an employee is found to be illegal or is in 
contravention of the prescribed procedure and that monetary compensation in lieu of reinstatement 
and back wages in cases of such nature may be appropriate. (See U.P. State Brassware Corpn. Ltd. 
v. Uday Narain Pandey [2006 (7) SCC 479], Uttaranchal Forest Development Corpn. v. M.C. 
Joshi [2007 (9) SCC 353], State of M.P. v. Lalit Kumar Verma [2007 (7) SCC 575], M.P. 
Admn. v. Tribhuban [2007 (9) SCC 748], Sita Ram v. Moti Lal Nehru Farmers Training 
Institute [2008 (5) SCC 75], Jaipur Development Authority v. Ramsahai [2006 (77) SCC 684], 
GDA vy. Ashok Kumar [2008 (4) SCC 26I] and Mahboob Deepak v. Nagar Panchayat, 
Gajraula [2008 (7) SCC 575].)" 


6.2. In subsequent decision in Rajasthan Development Corporation Vs.Gitam Singh (2073) 5 SCC 736॥, the 
Supreme Court stated, 


"From the long line of cases indicated above, it can be said without any fear of contradiction that 
this Court has not held as an absolute proposition that in cases of wrongful dismissal, the dismissed 
employee is entitled to reinstatement in all situations. It has always been the view of this Court that 
there could be circumstance(s) in a case which may make it inexpedient to order reinstatement. 
Therefore, the normal rule that the dismissed employee is entitled to reinstatement in cases of 
wrongful dismissal has been held to be not without exception. Insofar as wrongful termination of 
daily-rated workers is concerned, this Court has laid down that consequential relief would depend 
on host of factors, namely, manner and method of appointment, nature of employment and length of 
service. Where the length of engagement as daily wager has not been long, award of reinstatement 
should not follow and rather compensation should be directed to be paid. A distinction has been 
drawn between a daily wager and an employee holding the regular post for the purposes of 
consequential relief." 


6.3. In Uttaranchal Forest Development Corporation Vs. M.C. Joshi [(2007) 9 SCC 353], the Supreme Court 
held that the question of grant of compensation in place of relief of reinstatement could be guided by 
relevant factors to be that whether the appointment was made in accordance with the statutory Rules or not. 


6.4. It is to be observed that the decisions of the Supreme Court have carved out the circumstances and 


[भाग [ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 3, 2025/ज्येष्ठ 0, 947 3687 


aspects which may guide the discretion of the court in awarding lump-sum compensation instead of granting 
relief of reinstatement even if there is a breach of Section 25F, 25G and 25H of the Industrial Disputes Act. 


6.5. These factors were highlighted in Bantva Municipality Vs. Amritlal Harji Chauhan being Special Civil 
Application +०.9733 of 2973 decided on 37.3.2944 as under :- 


"(i) The fact that the workman is daily-rated workmen, not permanently employed; (ii) He is not 
holding a permanent post; (iii) Nature of his employment; (iv) Span of service, viz. The period 
during which he worked upto the date of termination of services; (v) Manner and method of 
appointment. Whether it was a backdoor entry; (vi) The time gap from the date of termination; (vii) 
Delay in raising the Reference is also considered to be a germane factor;(viii) Any special feature 
peculiar to the facts of the particular case. 


For instance, in Bhurumal (supra), the Supreme Court noticed that post which the workman held was of 
Lineman in the Telephone Department, and that the work of Lineman was drastically reduced in view of 
advancement of the technology." 


6.6. In the case of BSNL v. Bhurumal, reported in (2074) 7 SCC 777, it was categorically observed that even 
after reinstatement, it is always open to the management to terminate the services of that employee by paying 
him the retrenchment compensation. Even as a daily-wage worker, no useful purpose is going to be served in 
reinstating such a workman and he can be given monetary compensation by the Court itself.” 


In the case of State of Orissa vs. Mamata Mohanty reported in (2077) 3 SCC 436, the Hon’ble Supreme Court has 
held that the appointment made without advertisement was in violation of Article 4 and [6 of the Constitution. Para 
35 and 36 of the said judgment is reproduced below as follows:- 


"35. At one time this Court had been of the view that calling the names from Employment Exchange 
would curb to certain extent the menace of nepotism and corruption in public employment. But, later on, 
came to the conclusion that some appropriate method consistent with the requirements of Article 
46 should be followed. In other words there must be a notice published in the appropriate manner 
calling for applications and all those who apply in response thereto should be considered fairly. Even if 
the names of candidates are requisitioned from Employment Exchange, in addition thereto it is 
mandatory on the part of the employer to invite applications from all eligible candidates from the open 
market by advertising the vacancies in newspapers having wide circulation or by announcement in 
Radio and Television as merely calling the names from the Employment Exchange does not meet the 
requirement of the said Article of the Constitution. (Vide: Delhi Development Horticulture Employees’ 
Union v. Delhi Administration, Delhi & Ors., AIR /992 SC 789; State of Haryana & Ors. v. Piara Singh 
& Ors., AIR 7992 SC 27/30, Excise Superintendent Malkapatnam, Krishna District, A.P. v. K.B.N. 
Visweshwara Rao & Ors., (7996) 6 SCC 276, Arun Tewari & Ors. v. Zila Mansavi Shikshak Sangh & 
Ors., AIR 7996 SC 33l; Binod Kumar Gupta & Ors. 9. Ram Ashray Mahoto & Ors., AIR 2005 SC 
2/093, National Fertilizers Ltd. & Ors. v. Somvir Singh, AIR 2006 SC 2379, Telecom District Manager 
& Ors. v. Keshab Deb, (2008) 8 SCC 402; State of Bihar v. Upendra Narayan Singh & Ors., (2009) 5 
SCC 65; and State of Madhya Pradesh & Anr. v. Mohd. Ibrahim, (2009) 75 SCC 2/4,. 


Therefore, it is a settled legal proposition that no person can be appointed even on a temporary or ad 
hoc basis without inviting applications from all eligible candidates. If any appointment is made by 
merely inviting names from the Employment Exchange or putting a note on the Notice Board etc. that 
will not meet the requirement of Articles उर्ब and 76 of the Constitution. Such a course violates the 
mandates of Articles 44 and 76 of the Constitution of India as it deprives the candidates who are eligible 
for the post, from being considered. A person employed in violation of these provisions is not entitled to 
any relief including salary. For a valid and legal appointment mandatory compliance of the said 
Constitutional requirement is to be fulfilled. The equality clause enshrined in Article 6 requires that 
every such appointment be made by an open advertisement as to enable all eligible persons to compete 
on merit."
