AWARD 


In exercise of powers conferred under clause (d) of Sub-section () and Sub section (2A) of Section 0 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, !947 (4 of 947), the Government of India through the Ministr of Labour, vide its Order 
No. L-2202/37/2022-IR (CMII) dated 25/04/2022 has been pleased to refer the following dispute between the 
employer, that is the Management of Naba Kajora Colliery, Kajora Area of Eastern Coalfields Limited and their 
workmen for adjudication by this Tribunal. 


“Whether the demand raised by Koyala Mazdoor Congress (the union) against the Management of Kajora 
Area of M/s. Eastern Coalfields Ltd. for providing employment on compassionate ground to Shri Siddhant 
Murmu, dependent son of Late Bablu Murmu, ExTimber Mazdoor of Nav Kajora Colliery under Kajora Area 
of ECL, who died on 44/03/2077 while in service, is proper, legal and justified? If yes, to what relief Shri 
Siddhant Murmu, dependent son of Late Bablu Murmu is entitled to?” 


l. On receiving Order No. L-2202/37/2022-IR(CM-ID dated 25/04/2022 from the Government of India, Ministry of 

Labour, New Delhi for adjudication of the dispute, a Reference case No. l2 of 2022 was registered on 
26.04.2022/0.07.2022 and an order was passed for issuing notice to the parties through registered post, directing 
them to appear and submit their written statements along with relevant documents in support of their claims. 


2. Management of ECL filed written statement on [4/[/2022. Koyala Mazdoor Congress filed written statement on 
behalf of Sidhanta Murmu, dependent son of Late Bablu Murmu on 26/04/2023. Fact of the case disclosed in written 
statement of the union is that Bablu Murmu, Ex-Timber Mazdoor bearing UM No. 537444 was posted at Naba Kajora 
Colliery under Eastern Coalfields Limited (hereinafter referred as ECL). Bablu Murmu died in harness on 4/03/207 
leaving behind Lakhi Rani Murmu, his wife, Sidhanta Murmu his son, Sundari Murmu and Dulali Murmu, his two 
daughters and Kamali Murmu his mother. It is the case of the union that according to the provision of clause 9.3.2 of 
NCWA, a dependent of the workman who died in harness is entitled to get employment. Wife of the deceased 
submitted an application dated |/04/207 informing death of Bablu Murmu and also claimed employment for the 
son of the deceased. It is sated that on the date of death of the employee, Sidhanta Murmu was less than thirty five 


3722 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 3], 2025/JY AISTHA 0, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


years of age. Management arranged for “screening” at the colliery and area level and referred the dependent son for 
holding his medical examination by Initial Medical Examination Board. Medical Examination by IME Board was 
held on 22/02/209 and age of the dependent son was assessed as thirty four to thirty nine years as on 22/02/20]9 i.e. 
thirty six years six months as on 22/02/209, which is the mean of the assessed age ranging from thirty four to thirty 
nine years. Sidhanta Murmu was also declared medically fit for employment. On the basis of age assessed by Initial 
Medical Examination Board on 22/02/209, age of dependent son was thirty four years six months and twenty days 
on the date of death of Bablu Murmu i.e. on [4/03/207 and on the date of application for employment his age was 
thirty four years seven months and nineteen days. It is further stated that as per School Certificate date of birth of 
Sidhanta Murmu is 0/04/985 as such he was less than thirty five years on the date of death of his father. Proposal 
for employment was sent to ECL, Head Quarters with recommendation of General Manager of the Area but the 
management at Head Quarters did not consider the proposal for his employment on the ground that Sidhanta Murmu 
was above thirty five years of age on the date of submission of documents. Dependent son prayed for review of 
decision and he was referred to the Apex Medical Board for his age determination. Apex Medical Board increased the 
age of the dependent son by further six years than what was decided by Initial Medical Examination Board and 
regretted his prayer for employment. The dependent son claimed for his employment and monetary compensation to 
his mother till employment is provided to him under NCWA. 


3. Management in written statement admitted the fact that Bablu Murmu was a permanent employee of ECL and he 
was admitted to Central Hospital, Kalla before death on 4/03/20!7. Sidhanta Murmu submitted an application on 
24/04/20I8 claiming employment. His screening was done at Unit level on 27/lI/20i8 and Initial Medical 
Examination was held on 22/02/209. Initial Medical Examination Board assessed his age between thirty four years 
to thirty nine years as on 22/02/209 and he was found fit for job but due to overage, Sidhanta Murmu was not found 
eligible for employment as per the provision of NCWA. It is further stated in written statement that according to 
NCWA minimum age for employment of dependentsson/legally adopted son is eighteen years on the date of death of 
the employee and maximum age is thirty five years as on the date of application. According to the management date 
of birth of Sidhanta Murmu was assessed as 22/08/982 and on the date of death of employee, he was thirty four years 
six months and twenty two days of age and age of the claimant on date of submission of application was thirty five 
years eight months and two days. As claimant has exceeded maximum age stated in NCWA his application for 
compassionate appointment was not considered. Sidhanta Murmu applied forhis age assessment by the Apex Medical 
Board which was held on 05/03/202 and the Apex Medical Board assessed his age between forty to forty five years 
as on 05/03/202 so age of the claimant on the date of death of the employee was thirty eight years six months and 
nine days. Furthermore, it is contended that in Service Record Excerpt age of dependent son was recorded as five 
years as on 0/04/987, therefore, it is apparent that claimant was more than thirty five years on the date of death of 
his father. Management referred to the decision of Hon’ble High Court at Calcutta in the matter of Nemai Kumar 
Vs. CIL and Others, wherein the Hon’ble Court upheld decision of ECL in rejecting the claim of dependent on the 
ground of delay. It is inter alia contended that Hon’ble Supreme Court disapproved employment on compassionate 
ground after passage of long year. Management urged that in order to provide employment on compassionate ground 
claimant needs to fulfil eligibility and it cannot be granted in the form of concession. Management urged that there is 
no merit in the Industrial Dispute and the same is required to be dismissed. 


4. Short point for consideration before this Tribunal is “Whether the demand raised by Koyala Mazdoor Congress (the 
union) against the Management of Kajora Area of Eastern Coalfields Ltd. for providing employment on 
compassionate ground to Shri Sidhanta Murmu, dependent son of Late Bablu Murmu, Ex-Timber Mazdoor of Naba 
Kajora Colliery under Kajora Area of ECL, who died on 4/03/207 while in service, is 


proper, legal and justified? If yes, to what relief Shri Sidhanta Murmu, dependent son of Late Bablu Murmu 
is entitled to?” 


5. In order to prove their case, union filed an affidavit-in-chief of Sidhanta Murmu and examined him as Workman 
Witness-I. Witness reiterated his case disclosed in written statement and produced the following documents: 


(i) Copy of death certificate of his father issued by Central Hospital, Kalla is produced as Exhibit W-I. 
(ii) Copy of Death Registration Certificate of his father is produced as Exhibit W-2. 
(iii)Copy of service record of Bablu Murmu is produced as Exhibit W-3. 


(iv) Copy of application dated |/04/20!7 submitted by Lakhi Rani Murmu, his mother for providing employment to 
him is produced as Exhibit W-4. 


(v) Copy of proposal form issued by the management of Naba Kajora Colliery in two pages is collectively produced 
as Exhibit W-5. 


(vi) Copy of Transfer Certificate issued by Gourangdi R.K.S. Institution (H.S.) is produced as Exhibit W-6. 
(vii) Copy of letter dated | /08/2020 issued by the Agent, Naba Kajora Colliery is produced as Exhibit W-7. 


[भाग avs 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 3, 2025/ज्येष्ठ 0, 947 3723 


(viii) Copy of Medical Examination Report (IME) dated 22/02/209 is produced as Exhibit W-8. 

(ix) Copy of application dated 25/08/2020 addressed to the Agent, Naba Kajora Colliery is produced as Exhibit W-9. 
(x) Copy of letter regretting employment, issued by the Chief Manager (Personnel) is produced as Exhibit ४४-0. 
(xi) Copy of application requesting the management for review of the decision is produced as Exhibit W-I]. 

(xii) Copy of death certificate of his mother is produced as Exhibit ४४७-2. 

(xiii) Copy of circular dated 25/07/2003 is produced as Exhibit ४४-3. 

(xiv) Xerox copy of Aadhar Card is produced as Exhibit ४४-4. 

(xv) Xerox copy of PAN card is produced as Exhibit ४४-5. 


In-crossexamination, witness stated that an application was submitted on |[/04/207 by his mother, within one month 
from date of death of his father. He stated that according to Initial Medical Examination report his age was calculated 
as more than thirty five years and he was found overage. Witness admitted that he was referred to the Apex Medical 
Board on 05/03/202] and on examination by the concerned Medical Board, a report was prepared which has been 
identified as Exhibit M!. Witness denied that on the date of death of his father, his age was thirty eight years six 
months and nine days. It was admitted by WWI that he submitted another application dated 20/04/208 for his 
employment and denied suggestion that application dated /04/207 (Exhibit W4) was a manufactured document or 
it was not submitted before any representative of ECL. He denied suggestion that he was not entitled to get 
employment due to death of his father in harness. 


6. Mr. Ramjee Tripathi has been examined as Management Witness-I. He filed an affidavit-inchief supporting the 
case of management that Sidhanta Murmu crossed the upper age limit as per clause 9.3.4 of NCWA. It is further 
stated that on !/08/2020, Agent, Naba Kajora Colliery issued a letter informing Sidhanta Murmu that he was not 
eligible for employment for being overage. A copy of letter is produced as Exhibit M2. Witness stated that after 
receiving regret letter, the claimant submitted an application dated 25/08/2020 addressed to the Agent, Naba Kajora 
Colliery for reviewing prayer for employment by referring him to the Apex Medical Board. A copy of letter is 
produced as Exhibit M3. Witness deposed that Apex Medical Board submitted its report which has been produced as 
Exhibit M4 and by letter dated 07/05/202l (Exhibit M5) issued by the Chief Manager (Personnel) addressed to the 
General Manager, Kajora Area it has been informed that Sidhanta Murmu is not eligible for employment as per 
NCWA for being overage and the Competent Authority regretted his claim for employment. Service Excerpt of Bablu 
Murmu in two pages is collectively produced as Exhibit M6 and a copy of application submitted by Sidhanta Murmu 
seeking employment is produced as Exhibit M7. Copy of Initial Medical Examination report dated 22/02/209 is 
produced as Exhibit M8 and copy of Death Registration Certificate of Bablu Murmu is produced as Exhibit M9. In 
crossmexamination, witness deposed that Sidhanta Murmu submitted his first application on 24/04/20I8. In course of 
evidence he admitted that first application was submitted by the wife of the deceased on !/04/207 (Exhibit W4) and 
in the said letter she had claimed employment for her son. Witness could not state the date on which management 
issued letter to Sidhanta Murmu asking him to submit documents. Witness also produced a report of screening test 
held on 27//208 and it has been admitted in evidence as Exhibit Ml0. Witness denied suggestion that on 
/04/207 Sidhanta Murmu, son of the deceased was thirty four years seven months and seventeen days of age or 
that he was less than thirty five years of age. Witness also denied suggestion that age of Sidhanta Murmu assessed by 
the Apex Medical Board after two years was increased by four years. 


7.Mr. Rakesh Kumar, union representative referring to clause 9.3.4 of NCWA argued that dependent of the deceased 
employee who is physically fit should not be more than thirty five years of age as on date of death of employee. In the 
instant case Bablu Murmu died on [4/03/20]7 and death information and claim for employment was submitted by 
Lakhi Rani Murmu on ]/04/207 i.e. within one month from the date of death of employee. It is argued that 
Management Representative received a copy of application and Management Witness admitted in cross-examination 
that first application informing death of Bablu Murmu was submitted by his wife on /04/20l7 (Exhibit W-4). 
Therefore, in suggestion put to workman witness in his cross-examination that application dated | [/04/207 (Exhibit 
W-4) is a manufactured document or that it was not submitted before the representative of the company was 
unfounded and a futile attempt to disown responsibility. Mr. Rakesh Kumar argued that there is no dispute that 
Sidhanta Murmu is the son of Bablu Murmu, which would be evident from the service record excerpt of the 
employee. He appeared before the screening committee and was referred for medical examination by Initial Medical 
Examination Board on 22/02/209 (Exhibit 8). Initial Medical Examination Board found him fit for job and on the 
basis of appearance, the Medical Board assessed his age between thirty four years to thirty nine years on the date of 
assessment. According to the union on the date of death of his father, the claimant was thirty four years six months 
and twenty days of age, that is below thirty five years of age and he satisfied the eligibility criteria for employment. 
Mr. Kumar urged for passing of necessary direction upon the management of ECL to provide employment to the 
dependent son without further delay. It is inter alia argued that management cannot take advantage of their own fault 
by denying employment to the dependent son of the employee on the ground of delay as it is the management who 
committed delay by not considering the prayer made in April, 20l7 and by sending regret later on 07/05/202] 


3724 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 3], 2025/JY AISTHA 0, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


(Exhibit M-5). Union representative also claimed for payment of Monetary Compensation to the wife of the deceased 
till employment provided to their dependent son. 


8. Mr. P. K. Das, learned advocate for the management argued that Sidhanta Murmu is not entitled to get employment 
on the ground of delay as he has crossed the maximum age for getting employment to a male dependent. 


9. Ihave considered the rival arguments in light of the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence adduced 
by both parties. From the cross-examination of MW-I it is gathered that for the first time application informing death 
of the employee was submitted on !/04/207 (Exhibit W-4) by the wife of the deceased and she also claimed 
employment for their dependent son. After the employment process has been set in motion, it is the responsibility of 
the management to take step within time and decide upon the claim for employment raised by the dependent family 
members of the deceased. In the instant case management arranged for screening of family members of the deceased, 
Bablu Murmu on 27/I/20i8. Screening report has been admitted in evidence as Exhibit M-l0. Dependents of the 
deceased employee were identified and their signatures and left thumb Impressions were obtained. Medical 
Examination of the dependent son was held on 22/02/209 where his age was assessed as thirty four years to thirty 
nine years on the basis of his appearance which implied that on the date of death of his father, age of the dependent 
son was thirty four years six months and twenty days and on the date of submitting application on |/04/207 for 
employment his age was thirty four years seven months and nineteen days. Clause 9.3.4 of NCWA is silent about time 
of reckoning of the maximum age of the dependent for his employment. It is neither stated that age should be 
considered on the date of death of the employee nor on the date of submission of application. Union has produced a 
copy of circular dated 25/07/2003 issued by the Director (Pers. & IR) addressed to the Director (P), ECL, Sanctoria 
(Exhibit W-I3), wherein it is mentioned that NCWA has prescribed the age limit for appointment of eligible 
dependents. Hon’ble Minister replying to the question raised by the Hon’ble Members before the Consultative 
Committee meeting held on 23/05/2003has clarified that “the age on the date of application would be reckoned for 
offering employment on compassionate ground so that candidates are not debarred on the ground of age at the time of 
appointment.” It is therefore clear that for the purpose of reckoning eligibility, age of a person on date of application 
claiming employment would be considered in all subsidiaries of Coal India Limited and not the age at the time when 
appointment is given. Under such circumstance, the date of submitting application for employment by the wife of 
deceased on |/04/207 claiming legal dues and employment to their son is the date for reckoning the date for 
application. I find that on that date age of Sidhanta Murmu on the basis of age assessed by the Medical Board on 
22/02/20l9 was less than thirty five years and he was also found fit for employment. In case of Bhawani Prasad 
Sonkar vs Union of India and Others (20l) 4 SCC 209; the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India has held that “Now, it is 
well settled that compassionate employment is given solely on humanitarian grounds with the sole object to provide 
immediate relief to the employee’s family to tide over the sudden financial crisis and cannot be claimed as a matter of 
right. Appointment based solely on descent is inimical to our Constitutional scheme, and ordinarily public 
employment must be strictly on the basis of open invitation of applications and comparative merit, in consonance with 
Articles 4 and l6 of the Constitution of India. No other mode of appointment is permissible. Nevertheless, the 
concept of compassionate appointment has been recognized as an exception to the general rule, carved out in the 
interest of justice, in certain exigencies, by way of a policy of an employer, which partakes the character of the 
service rules. That being so, it needs little emphasis that the scheme or the policy, as the case may be, is binding both 
on the employer and the employee. Being an exception, the scheme has to be strictly construed and confined only to 
the purpose it seeks to achieve.” 


0.In order to maintain a fair labour practice, company is duty bound to honour the terms and conditions it has agreed 
upon in NCWA. It is absolutely clear that when an employee dies in harness management of the company has to 
provide an employment to one dependent of the deceased who shall be within age limit of eighteen years to thirty five 
years of age and in case of female spouse, forty five years as provided in clause 9.5.0 and in so far male spouse is 
concerned, there would be no age limit in providing employment. Clarification has been provided for reckoning age 
of the claimant i.e. date of submission of application. From report of Initial Medical Examination, I find that Sidhanta 
Murmu was less than thirty five years of age and he was found medically fit for employment. There is no provision in 
NCWA to consider financial viability of candidate as a prerequisite for providing employment. Therefore, 
management cannot be allowed to harp upon any extraneous issue for debarring the dependent from getting benefit of 
employment. It also appears to me that delay caused in providing employment is attributable to the tardigrade 
approach of the management to deal with employment proposal and keep the same pending for several years without 
any communication to the claimant. Management cannot derive benefits for their own wrong. In the instant case 
family of the deceased had to wait without any employment for over seven years. In my considered view this is an 
appropriate case to allow Monetary Compensation to the female dependent i.e. wife of the deceased employee from 
4/03/207 till employment is granted to their dependent son or Lakhi Rani Murmu, widow attains sixty years of age, 
whichever is earlier. Management shall take appropriate step to provide employment to Sidhanta Murmu within three 
months from date of communication of the Award and 


also pay arrear of Monetary Compensation to the widow of the deceased employee. 


Hence, 


[भाग ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 3, 2025/ज्येष्ठ 0, 947 3725 


ORDERED 


that the Industrial Dispute is allowed on contest in favour of Sidhanta Murmu, dependent son of Late Bablu Murmu. 
Management of Naba Kajora Colliery shall provide employment to Sidhanta Murmu within three months from the 
date of communication of Award and shall also pay Monetary Compensation to Lakhi Rani Murmu, widow of the 
deceased from the date of death of Bablu Murmu, the employee till she attains sixty years of age or till employment is 
provided to their son, whichever is earlier. Let an Award be drawn up in light of my above findings. Let copies of 
Award be communicated to the Ministry for information and Notification.

l. The Reference belongs to CGIT-l, however as per the direction of the High Court, I am deciding this 
Reference. 


This is reference made by the Central Government in exercise of powers under clause (d) of sub-section (I) 
and sub-section (2A) of Section |0 of the Industrial Disputes Act, !947 vide Government of India, Ministry of Labour 
& Employment, New Delhi vide its order No. L-300/20/2008 — IR (M) dated 03.]].2008. The terms of reference 
given in the schedule are as follows: 


“Whether the action of the management of ONGC, Mumbai employing the 79 field operators in the offshore 
on fixed term employment is legal and justified? What relief these workmen are entitled to? And whether they 
are entitled for regularization as demanded by the Union?” 


2. Undisputedly originally this Industrial Dispute was raised on behalf of 79 employees however during 
pendency of Reference, the services of most of the employees were regularized by the first party ONGC, some of the 
employees resigned from the services of the first party ONGC, some employees died, stopped reporting for work and 
now only 9 employees, namely Ankush G. Katara, Liladhar M. Koli, Kailash 9. Dandekar, Sandeep D. Chari, Sunil T. 
Sakpal, Milind B. Parkar, Siddharth D. Bhika, Prashant D. Pawaskar & Abrar Ahmed Mohammed remained in the 
present Reference. 


3. The Second Party states that, the employees remained in the Reference are performing their duties since 
2000 & 200! at oil rigs of First Party ONGC, which is a mining industry engaged in exploring and producing natural 
gas, oil and petroleum products. The employees involved in the Reference are engaged as fixed term employees and 
performing their work continuously. They were appointed as assistant rigman, the work performed by them is 
perennial and regular nature and that post is of class-II, Grade-III employees. These employees are getting basic pay 
at par with permanent rigman, however there is difference in the allowances. The duties performed by these 
employees are highly skilled, operational and technical in nature. Subsequently the First Party ONGC changed the 
designation of assistant rigman to field operator with a view to deny parity, however there was no change in work. 
The First Party ONGC reduced the emoluments, allowances and benefits and this conduct of the First Party ONGC is 
illegal, unjustified and against the provisions of the standing orders. 


The Second Party further states that, the work performed by the employees is identical to the permanent 
employees, therefore they are entitled regularization at par with permanent employees alongwith all allowances. 
Though the appointment letter stipulates that, the appointment is for exigencies of work, however the said work is of 
permanent nature. In fact, the work of exploration and production of natural gas, oil and other petroleum products is 
growing work as demand is increasing, as such the work performed by the concerned employees is certainly not 
temporary or short term. The employees concerned in this Reference as well as permanent employees performed same 
work. The Second Party also states that, there is no justification for illegality of discriminating employees performing 
same and similar nature of work and the act of the first party ONGC is in breach of provisions of Act. The union has 
expousing this cause since long with the authorities under the Act, however during pendency of conciliation 
proceedings, the First Party ONGC had adversely changed the service conditions time to time under the grab of 
extending tenure/fresh appointment, therefore the ONGS has grossly highlighted the provisions of Sec.9-A as well as 
Sec.33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. Thus the Second Party prays for declaration that, the workmen involved in the 
Reference are permanent employees of the First Party ONGC and entitled to wages, benefits and allowance at par 
with permanent employees performing the same work and they be absolved as permanent workmen of ONGC from 
the date of completion of 240 days of continuous service and also pay wages, allowances and benefits at par with 
permanent employees, arrears of wages, allowances and benefits with 8% Interest. 


4. The First Party ONGC resisted the claim of the Second Party by reply. The First Party ONGC contends that, 
the concerned employees were employed under the contract employment, the offer of employment given by the First 
Party ONGC was accepted by the Second Party employees for consideration under Indian Contract Act, 872, thus 
rendering the employment justified. There is no Industrial Dispute between the parties within the meaning of 
Industrial Disputes Act. Similarly, the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act and other various laws of the country 
are not applicable beyond 2 Nauticals miles from the base line of Indian main land, therefore the Reference as 
framed is not maintainable. 


[भाग त--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 3, 2025/ज्येष्ठ 0, 947 3727 


The First Party ONGC further states that, they hired various persons as field operators for fixed term of four 
years in 2005, 2009 & employees appointed on tenure basis were selected under the recruitment process includes 
recruitment, advertisement, written test and interview. All fixed term employment is independent of each other and 
have no relation whatsoever. Those employees are getting benefits and wages as mentioned in the respective offers of 
engagement letter. Every employment expired on the date mentioned in the appointment letter and on expiry the 
person seized to be the contractual employment. The change of designation from assistant rigman to field operator 
was in accordance with the condition of appointment on tenure basis at non-executive level and the same is based on 
the level of skilled and qualification level. There was no change in the pattern of Provident Fund and Gratuity. The 
workmen continued to be governed by the relevant provisions of ONGC, Service Rules & CDA Rules 994 and there 
was no change of service conditions of tenure based employees. Tenure based employees are seeking a back door 
entry into the services of the First Party ONGC by demanding the regularization of their services. The workmen are 
required to follow procedures and qualifications prescribed in ONGC MR PR 980 for permanent employees and the 
workmen cannot ask to bypass or ignore the same. The entry in public sector undertaking should be on the basis of the 
selection process laid down in the establishment. 


The First Party ONGC also states that, the Tribunal does not have the jurisdiction to examine the terms and 
conditions offered to the tenure employees as it would amounts to interfere in the rights of the employer to choose the 
right persons/term of employment as would be suitable for their business model and no jurisdiction to compel any 
employer to conduct their business, there is no change of service condition as alleged nor any illegality on the part of 
the First Party and the Second Party is not entitled for regularization as claimed and ultimately prayed that, the 
Reference be answered in the negative.

6. Issue No. | & 2 - Both the issues are interrelated therefore answered together. 


It is worthwhile to mention here that, though the first party ONGC contended that, the provisions of the 
Industrial Dispute Act and other various laws of this country are not applicable beyond 2 Nauticals miles from the 
base line of Indian main land as such this court has no jurisdiction to adjudicate the present Reference and the 
Reference as framed is not tenable under law. 


However in fact, the first party ONGC in its reply has specifically stated that, the employees were employed 
under the contract of employment, the offer of employment given by the first party was accepted by the employee for 
consideration under the Indian Contract Act, it itself shows that, the Indian Contract Act is applicable to the present 
dispute. 


Furthermore, it reveals that, the first party ONGC published advertisement for the post hold by the 
employees within the Indian territories, the entire recruitment process was conducted within the Indian territory, Offer 
letters, Appointment letters and all other correspondence was issued within the Indian territories. All department of 
the first party ONGC are controlled from the Indian territories. The oil rigs upon which the employee involved in the 
Reference are performing duties belongs to first party ONGC. The policies concerning oil exploration are fixed within 
Indian territories. The disciplinary actions against employees performing duties upon oil rigs initiated and conducted 
in Indian territories in accordance with Indian law as such it will be unsafe to say and accept that, the Indian laws are 
not applicable to the first party ONGC. 


Similarly, the second party employee raised dispute in respect of their regularization against the fist party 
ONGC and considering the nature of dispute, it is certainly an Industrial Dispute as such this Tribunal has jurisdiction 


3726 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 3], 2025/JY AISTHA 0, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


to adjudicate the present industrial dispute as such the Reference as framed is tenable under law, and this Tribunal has 
jurisdiction to adjudicate the present Reference hence I answer these issues in the affirmative. 


7. Issue No. 3 - Both the parties have not adduced any oral evidence in the matter and the second party union put 
their reliance on the various copies of appointment orders available on record. 


On careful perusal of the various copies of appointment orders it reveals that, the Ankush Gopal Katara 
was initially appointed on the post of Asst. Rigman (D) by order dated 20 December 2000 on the recommendation of 
the selection committee and medical certificate issued by DGM (MS) for the period of three years, his appointment 
was for fixed period. Subsequently he was appointed by order dated 29.0].2005 for a fixed period of four years till 
3.0.2009, order dated 08.02.203 for a fixed period of four years, order dated 4.02.207 for a fixed period of four

08.03.207 and post at Rig Sagar Kiran.

committee for the post of Asst. Rigman (Drilling) dated 5..200l, he was appointed for a period of three years.

It is clear from the above discussed facts of employment of nine employees remained in the Reference that, 
all these employees were initially appointed as Asst. Rigman and subsequently engaged as Field Operators, which 
may be the promotional as well as higher post than Asst. Rigman. All these employees were sponsored by 
employment exchange, they were asked to appear for written test, they were called for oral interview before selection 
committee constituted by first party ONGC. Thereafter they were asked to appear for medical examination before the 
medical authority of first party ONGC and then only these employees were engaged in the employment of the first 
party ONGC as such the appointment of all these 9 employees were made after following due recruitment procedure 
required to follow for regular appointment in the establishment of the first party ONGC as such the appointments 
cannot be termed as illegal. 


On perusal of the various copies of orders placed on record by the second party union that, though the 
appointments of these employees was contractual and for fixed period of three to four years and their services were 
came to an end from the date mentioned in the appointment letters, however the counsel for the first party ONGC 
couldn’t substantiate the same that on what basis or rules such contractual appointments were made by the first party. 


It will not be out of place to mention here that, as per the Model Standing Orders (Central), the workmen are 
classified as permanent, probationers, badlis, temporary, casual and apprentices. It has been clarified that, temporary 
workman is a workman who has been engaged for work which is of essentially temporary nature likely to be finished 
within a limited period and casual workman is a workman whose employment is of casual nature. It goes to show that, 
the employee engaged and continued for years together cannot be termed as temporary or casual, more particularly 
when these employees worked more than I5 to 20 years with the first party ONGC as such it is clear that, these nine 
employees engaged and continued for years together cannot be termed as ‘temporary’ or ‘casuals’. 


Not only this but, it seems that, the work which is performed by these employees is also permanent in nature 
and continued years together. Initially the employees were engaged as Asst. Rigman and subsequently they were 
appointed as Field Operator. It is not the case of the first party ONGC that, the work on which these nine employees 
were working was temporary in nature nor the first party ONGC substantiate the fact about necessity of contractual 
employment of these employees for fix- period. It goes to show that, the work of Asst. Rigman and Field Operators 
performed by these employees was of permanent in nature. 


Furthermore, on perusal of the appointment orders it seems that, all these employees were given various 
allowances required to be given permanent employees except fixed wages during the period of employment. These 
employees were given Provident Fund and Gratuity as admissible to regular employee and there is a facility of earned 
leave, half pay leave and casual leave as applicable to regular employee and these employees are entitled for 
encasement of earned leave at credit and though their appointment was for fixed period but they continued in service 
without break. 


Similarly in the appointment letter there is mention about the post on which the employees were appointed 
and also about the period of employment, however there is no whisper in the order that, the appointment was for 
specific work or project. It is not the case of the first party ONGC that, the post on which these employees were 
appointed is temporary post and also not sanctioned post. Thus there is no hesitation to accept that, the appointment of 
these employees were against sanctioned post also. 


Much is argued on behalf of the first party ONGC that, the appointment of the employees involved in the 
Reference was contractual and not against the permanent post and allowing these employees in regular employment 
means allowing back door entry in the employment which is not permissible. The reliance has been placed on the 
decision of the Supreme Court in Secretary State of Karnataka & Ors. v/s. Umadevi and Ors. (2006) 4 SCC .I 
have gone through the same in which it has been appreciated that, allowing irregular appointment amounts to back 
door entry which is not permissible, however in the case in hand I have observed that, these employees were 
appointed after compliance of the prescribed procedure of the appointment. The same is against the post which is of 
permanent nature and it is not a back door entry in the employment of the first party ONGC therefore I do not think 
that, the appointment of the employees is illegal nor it was back door entry in the employment of the first party 
ONGC therefore the decision in case of Umadevi is not applicable. 


As discussed above it is clear that, the appointment of these employees was/is against sanctioned vacant 
posts, their appointment is not as temporary employee, they were recruited by following prescribed procedure of 
recruitment, therefore these appointments cannot be termed as back door, moreover the action of the first party ONGC 
employing these employees as Asst. Rigman and the field operators on fixed term appointment is not legal, hence I 
answer this issue in the negative. 


8. Issue No. 4 - It is sufficiently established before the Tribunal that, inspite of sanction post of Asst. Rigman and 
Field Operators, the first party ONGC gave contractual appointments to these employees involved in the Reference 


3730 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 3, 2025/JY AISTHA 0, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


and I have observed in the light of various decisions of High Court Ahmedabad in Spl. Civil Application No.2248, 
283,6777,444 & 283 of 20l2 ONGC Employees Mazdoor Sabha v/s. ONGC Ltd., Letters Patent Appeals 
No. 797 of 203 & Ors. Executive Director ONGC Ltd. v/s. ONGC Employees Mazdoor Sabha & 2., that the 
appointment of these employees is not back door entry. 


Undisputedly all these employees are in the employment of the first party ONGC since 2000 or 200 and 
certainly worked not only 240 days, but more than 240 days in every year of appointment, therefore these nine 
employees are entitled for permanency on the post of Asst. Rigman or Field Operators since the date of completion of 
240 days of their employment hence I answer this issue in the affirmative. 


In the result, I proceed to pass the following order- 
ORDER 
i. The Reference is answered in the affirmative. 
ii. The nine employees in the Reference are entitled for 
permanency as claimed. 
iii. The first party ONGC is hereby directed to make these 
employees namely Ankush G. Katara, Liladhar M. Koli,

completion of 240 days of their service and also the financial

the date of publication of Award.

(JUDGMENT) 


(Passed on this 23" day of April- 2025) 


As per letter dated 23/09/205 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference is 
made to this Tribunal under Section-l0 of Industrial Disputes Act, 947 (in short the ‘Act’)as per Notification 
No. L-2902/2/20I5 (IR(M)) dt. 23/09/205. The dispute under reference relates to: 


“Whether the action of the management of Managing Director, M.P. State Mining Corporation Ltd., 
Bhopal in terminating the services of workman Shri Keshav Prasad Tiwari w.e.f. 72.07.2077 is justified? If not, 
what relief the Workman is entitled to?” 


Notices were issued to the parties after registering the case on the basis of reference. They appeared and 
filed their respective statement of defense and claim. 


The undisputed facts are that, the Workman was appointed by the Management, in 982, was regularized in 
October, 989 and while he was working at Jhabua, he suffered an injury and was under treatment, hence he was 
absent from his workplace from 2.05.2005 to 2.08.2005. The Management stopped his two increments by way 
of punishment without accumulative effect. He was issued show cause notice on 02.02.20I], alleging that he was 
unauthorisedly absent from 08.06.200 till date of notice and was asked to show cause why disciplinary action 
should not be taken against him. He submitted his reply on 4.03.20 in which he stated that, it was due to his 
illness and sickness of his mother, he could not attend his duty and filed medical certificates in this respect before 
the Management. The Management then issued a show cause notice alleging the charge of unauthorized absence 
against the Workman on 08.04.20I] to which the Workman submitted his reply which he had already submitted 
and requested heard personal hearing, which he was not accorded and without inquiry he was punished with 
termination of his services by Management which is unjust, illegal and arbitrary. As it was a major punishment 
imposed on him without any Departmental Enquiry. 


Management has defended its action with the case, that the reply of the Workman to the show cause notice 
was not found sufficient he was accorded personal hearing also, but he could not satisfy the Management 
regarding the reasons of his absence, and then his services were terminated by Management vide its order dated 
02.07.20]. 


Documents filed by the parties are admitted by both the parties, which are termination order and show 
cause notice as well the charge sheet. Both the sides have filed their affidavit as their examination-in-chief. 


I have heard argument of Learned Counsel for the Workman Mr. Pranay Choubey. None appeared for 
Management. Workman has filed written arguments also. I have gone through the written arguments and the 
record. 


On perusal of record it comes out that, the workman was issued a show cause notice in form of a charge 
sheet and he filed his reply in which he denied the charges and narrated about the circumstances about his alleged 
willful and unauthorized absence from workplace. There was no formal Departmental Enquiry was conducted by 
Management to inquire into the depth of allegations and defense. Now, the question arises for consideration is 
whether the action of Management in terminating the services of the Workman without conducting any formal 
enquiry on charges of misconduct, is justified in law or not? 


Reference may be made to Article ३3]] of Constitution of India which is being reproduced as follows : 


“ (7) No person who is a member of a civil service of the Union or an all-India service or a civil 
service of a State or holds a civil post under the Union or a State shall be dismissed or removed 
by an authority subordinate to that by which he was appointed. 


(2) No such person as aforesaid shall be dismissed or removed or reduced in rank until he has 
been given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in 
regard to him: 


Provided that this clause shall not apply— 


3732 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 3], 2025/JY AISTHA 0, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


(a) where a person is dismissed or removed or reduced in rank on the ground of conduct which has led to 
his conviction on a criminal charge; 


(b) where an authority empowered to dismiss or remove a person or to reduce him in rank is satisfied that 
for some reason, to be recorded by that authority in writing, it is not reasonably practicable to give to that 
person an opportunity of showing cause; or 


(c) where the President or Governor or Rajpramukh, as the case may be, is satisfied that in the interest of 
the security of the State it is not expedient to give to that person such an opportunity. 


(3) If any question arises whether it is reasonably practicable to give to any person an 
opportunity of showing cause under clause (2), the decision thereon of the authority empowered 
to dismiss or remove such person or to reduce him in rank, as the case may be, shall be final.” 


It is established from the perusal of Article 3l, that the case of employee was not covered in the cases in 
which a formal Departmental Enquiry could be dispensed with by the Appointing Authority. 


Hence, on the basis of above discussion, the order of termination issued by MP State Mining Corporation 
by way of punishment vide its order dated 02,07.2077, to the Workman Keshav Prasad Tiwari is held vitiated in 
law setting aside the punishment order, the Workman Keshav Prasad Tiwari is reinstated in service from 
42.07.2077 and shall be deemed in regular services by Management till date or till date of his superannuation 
whichever is earlier but without back wages. He shall be entitled to all the in service and post retiral benefits, 
treating himself in continuous services as mentioned above payable to him with in thirty days from the date of 
publication of this award failing which interest of 8% p.a. from the date of award till payment. There shall be 
no order as to cost. 


The reference stands answered accordingly.

AWARD 
(Passed on this 22™ day of April-2025.) 


The workman has filed this petition u/s. 2-A (2&3) of the Industrial Disputes Act 947 (in short ‘The Act”) 
against termination of his services by the respondents/management. 


After registering the case on the basis of the petition, notices were sent to management and were duly served 
on them. They appeared and filed their statements of defense. 


The case of the workman, in short, is that he was appointed as Business Development Executive-IV by the 
opposite party on !7.02.20l0 and was posted in Bhopal. He continued for six years as such till 04.06.20l6 when his 
services were terminated by management without any notice or compensation or any inquiry which is unjust, illegal 
and arbitrary on the part of management. He has prayed that holding the termination of his services by management, 
he be held entitled to be reinstated with back wages and benefits. 


The case of the management, inter alia, is that, firstly, the petitioner was appointed for Marketing of 
Products, hence he is not a workman as define u/s. 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act, !947 (in short the ‘Act’) and 
secondly, his appointment was fixed term appointment which was not extended after completion of tenure, thus not 
retrenchment as defined u/s. 2(00) of the Act. 


In evidence, the workman filed the certificate regarding failure of conciliation issued by the RLC, his 
appointment letter dated !7.02.20l0 with terms of appointment and disengagement letter dated 04.06.206, admitted 
by management. 


Management has not filed any document or affidavit. 


I have heard argument of learned Counsel Mr. Ashok Shrivastava. None appeared for arguments for 
management. Management filed written arguments which are on record. I have gone through the written arguments 
and the records as well. 


On perusal of record, in the light of rival arguments, following issues arise for determination :- 


हे Whether, the petitioner is a workman as defined u/s. 26) of the Act ? 
Whether, the termination of services of the petitioner is retrenchment as defined u/s. 2(00) of the Act and 
is bad in law ? 

3. Whether, the petitioner is entitled to any relief ? 


Issue No. l. 
Section 2(s) of the Act, which defines Workman, is being reproduced as follows: 


3734 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 3], 2025/JY AISTHA 0, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


“2(s) “workman” means any person including an apprentice employed in any industry to do any manual, unskilled, 
skilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory work for hire or reward, whether the terms of employment be 
express or implied, and for the purposes of any proceeding under this Act in relation to an industrial dispute, includes 
any such person who has been dismissed, discharged or retrenched in connection with, or as a consequence of, that 
dispute, or whose dismissal, discharge or retrenchment has led to that dispute, but does not include any such person— 


(i) who is subject to the Air Force Act, 950 (45 of 950), or the Army Act, 950 (46 of 950), or the Navy Act, 957 
(62 of 957); or 


(ii) who is employed in the police service or as an officer or other employee of a prison; or 
(iii) who is employed mainly in a managerial or administrative capacity; or 
(iv) who, being employed in a supervisory capacity, draws wages exceeding ten thousand rupees per mensum or 


exercises, either by the nature of the duties attached to the office or by reason of the powers vested in him, functions 
mainly of a managerial nature...................seeeee eee 


Learned Senior Counsel for Petitioner has relied on judgment of Hon’ble High Court of Bombay in the case of 
Union Carbide (India) Ltd. V.s. Ramesh Kumbla and Others reported in MANU/MH/0073/999 and another 
judgment of the same High Court in the case of Union Carbide (India) Ltd. V.s. D. Samuel and Others 
reported in MANU/MH/73/998. 


In these two cases, after analyzing the judgment of various High Courts and Hon’ble Supreme Court, the Single 
Bench of Hon’ble Bombay High Court has summarized the principles on the basis of which it is to be decided 
whether the Workman is in supervisory capacity or not. These tests mentioned in Para 34 and 35 of the Judgment are 
being reproduced as follows: 


“Para-34. In so far as the Apex Court is concerned, some of the tests laid down are: 

(6) Designation is not material but what is important is the nature of work. 

(2) Find out the dominant purpose of employment and not any additional duties the employee may be 
performing. 

(3) Can he bind the Company/employer to some kind of decisions on behalf of the Company/employer. 

(4) Has the employee power to direct or oversee the work of his subordinates. 

(5) Has the power to sanction leave or recommend it; and 

(6) Has he the power to appoint, terminate or take disciplinary action against workmen. 


Para-35. From the judgment of this Court and the other High Courts some of the tests apart from what the 
Apex Court has stated are: 


(a) Whether the employee can examine the quality of work and whether such work is performed in 
satisfactory manner or not; 

(b) Does the employee have powers of assigning duties and distribution of work; 

(c) Can he indent material and distribute the same amongst the workmen; 

(d) Even though he has no authority to grant leave does he have power to recommend leave; 

(e) Are there persons working under him; 

(f) Has he the power to supervise the work of men and not merely machines; 

(g) Dos he mark the attendance of other employees; 

(h) Does he write the confidential reports of his subordinates.” 


Learned Counsel for management has referred to Judgment of Hon’ble High Court of MP in W.A. No. 75/20I7 
Novartis India Vs. Vipin Shrivastava, wherein a Division Bench of Hon’ble High Court has held that, since the 
petitioner in the referred case was engaged as a sales representative in a Pharmaceutical Company, his duty was to 
visit Doctors, Chemist, as well Stockists, meeting different professionals to promote sale, his job being not manual or 
clerical, hence though he might not be controlling any subordinates, he was master of his work assigned with respect 
to performance of job being solemnly in his discretion, he was not a workman as defined u/s. 2(s) of the Act. 


In another judgment of Hon’ble the Supreme Court referred to the Burmah Shell Oil Storage and Distributing 
Company vs. Burmah Shell Management Staff Association, (7970) 3 SCC 378, in which a full Bench of Hon’ble 
Supreme Court held that the petitioner who was appointed as a District Sales Representative, his job being making of 
recommendations for selection of agents and dealers in connection with promotion of sale, extension or curtailment of 
credit facilities to agent, dealers and customers; investment on capital and revenue in shape of facilities at agent 
premises or retail outlets and selection of suitable sites for retails outlets to maximize sales and negotiations for terms 
of new sites he could not be classified as a workman as defined u/s. 2(s) of the Act. 


Now, coming to the facts of case in hand, in the light of above proposition of law, the appointment letter of 


[भाग त---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 3, 2025/ज्येष्ठ 0, 947 3735 


the workman which he accepted and was appointed as Business Development Executive-IV. His job was with respect 
to marketing and sales. After accepting the terms and conditions in the offer of appointment letter. 


In the light of above facts & proposition of law as mentioned above, the petitioner is held not be a workman 
as defined u/s. 2(s) of the Act. 


Reference of Section 6 of Sales Promotion Employees Condition of Service Act 976 also requires to be 
made here which is being reproduced as follows:- 


Application of certain Acts to sales promotion employees.— 
(7) The provisions of the Workmen’s Compensation Act, /923 (8 of /923) as in force for the time being, shall 
apply to, or in relation to, sales promotion employees as they apply to, or in relation to, workmen within the 
meaning of that Act. 


(2) The provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 7947 (74 of 7947), as in force for the time being, shall 
apply to, or in relation to, sales promotion employees as they apply to, or in relation to, workmen within the 
meaning of that Act and for the purposes of any proceeding under that Act in relation to an industrial 
dispute, a sales promotion employee shall be deemed to include a sales promotion employee who has been 
dismissed, discharged or retrenched in connection with, or as a consequence of, that dispute or whose 
dismissal, discharge or retrenchment had led to that dispute. 


(3) The provisions of the Minimum Wages Act, /9246 (77 of /946), as in force for the time being, shall apply to, 
or in relation to, sales promotion employees as they apply to, or in relation to, employees within the meaning of 
that Act. 


(4) The provisions of the Maternity Benefit Act, /967 (53 of /964), as in force for the time being, shall apply to, 
or in relation to, sales promotion employees, being women, as they apply to, or in relation to, women employed, 
whether directly or through any agency, for wages in any establishment within the meaning of that Act. 


(5) The provisions of the Payment of Bonus Act, /9635 (27 of 79635), as in force for the time being, shall apply to, 
or in relation to, sales promotion employees as they apply to, or in relation to, employees within the meaning of 
that Act. 


(6) The provisions of the Payment of Gratuity Act, /972 (39 of 79/2), as in force for the time being, shall apply 
to, or in relation to, sales promotion employees as they apply to, or in relation to, employees within the meaning 
of that Act. 
(7) Notwithstanding anything contained in the foregoing sub-sections,— 
(a) in the application of any Act referred to in any of the said sub-sections to sales promotion employees, the 
wages of a sales promotion employee for the purposes of such Act, shall be deemed to be his wages as 
computed in accordance with the provisions of this Act; 
(b) where an Act referred to in any of the said sub-sections provides for a ceiling limit as to wages so as to 
exclude from the purview of the application of such Act persons whose wages exceed such ceiling limit, such 
Act shall not apply to any sales promotion employee whose wages as computed in accordance with the 
provisions of this Act exceed such ceiling limit. 
Hence, it is held that though the workman is not a workman as defined u/s. 2(s) of the Act but by virtue of 
Section 6 of Sales Promotion Employees Conditions of Service Act 976, as mentioned above, the provisions of 
the Industrial Disputes Act 947 shall apply in his case. 

Issue No.-| is answered accordingly. 

Issue No.-2 :- 


Section 2(00) of the Act is being reproduced as follows :- 


(00) “retrenchment” means the termination by the employer of the service of a workman for any any 
reason whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action, but does not 
include— 

(a) voluntary retirement of the workman; or 

(b) retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of employment 


between the employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulation in that behalf; or 


(bb) termination of the service of the workman as a result of the non-renewal of the contract of 
employment between the employer and the workman concerned on its expiry or of such contract being 
terminated under a stipulation in that behalf contained therein; or 

(c) termination of the service of a workman on the ground of continued ill-health; 

As it transpires from evidence, the appointment of the workman was for a fixed term of one year which was 
extended on yearly basis till 07.06.20l6. This service contract was terminated by management and he was 
disengaged on 04.06.20I6 i.e. three days before completion of the contract, in the light of Clause-2 of the 
Service Contract which mentions that during the contract period, his services will be liable to be terminated 


3736 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : MAY 3, 2025/JY AISTHA 0, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


without assigning any reason or giving any notice. In the light of these facts, termination of his service contract 
cannot be said to be retrenchment as defined u/s. 2(00) of the Act. 


Issue no.-2 is answered accordingly. 
Issue No.-3:- 
In the light of findings recorded above, the workman is held entitled to no relief. 
In the light of findings recorded above, the petition stands disposed accordingly. 
No order as to Cost.

(JUDGMENT) 


(Passed on this day of April- 2025) 


As per letter dated 0/06/205 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference is 
made to this Tribunal under Section-l0 of Industrial Disputes Act, |947 (in short the ‘Act’)as per Notification 


[भाग ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : मई 3, 2025/ज्येष्ठ 0, 947 3737 


No. L-2602/7/205 (IR(M)) dt. 0/06/205. The dispute under reference relates to: 


“Whether the action of the management of Bhilai Steel Plant in dismissing the service of Sh. Dhani Ram, 
Ex-Sr. Operative Gr. 2 w.e.f. /0.77.20/4 is justified? If not, what relief the Workman should get?” 


Notices were issued to the parties after registering the case on the basis of reference. They appeared and 
filed their respective statement of defense and claim. 


Case of the Workman is that, he was charged by unauthorized and willful absence from Workplace within 
the period February, 20l3 to December, 20!3 for 47 days with respect to which the Departmental Enquiry was 
conducted against him. His defense was that, he was sick during that period. He produced documents regarding his 
sickness but Management got a letter regarding admission of the charge written by him and terminated his services. 
The Enquiry was unjust, illegal and proper. According to the Workman, charges were wrongly held proved and the 
punishment was disproportionate to the charge. 


Case of the Management is that, the Workman is in the habit of absenting himself without notice to 
management or without getting any leave sanctioned for which he has been punished five times, details mentioned in 
Para 4 of Written Statement after different enquiries, he did not improved himself and again absented himself 
unauthorizedly. The Enquiry Officer submitted his report after enquiry holding the charges proved and he was 
terminated from service keeping in view his past conduct. 


The following preliminary issue was framed on the basis of pleadings on .02.2020. 
Whether the Enquiry Conducted was legal and proper? 


During proceeding, the Workman died and he was represented by his legal representatives. The preliminary 
issue was decided defining the Enquiry legal and proper vide order dated 25.07.2024. This order is part of this 
judgment. 


Following additional issues were framed: 
4. Whether the charges are proved on the basis of enquiry? 
2. Whether the punishment is proportionate to the charges. 


Parties were required to lead evidence if any. They did not lead any evidence. I have heard argument of 
Learned Counsel for Management Mr. R.C. Shrivastava. None appeared from side of Workman. I have gone 
through the record. 


Additional Issue 'ब०.- 


It comes from pursuance of proved enquiry papers that Workman himself admitted the misconduct. His 
case in his pleading was only that, latter admitting misconduct was got signed under undue influence. The burden 
lies on him to prove this fact in which he had failed, hence, findings of the Enquiry Officer that the charges are 
proved cannot be faulted with. 


Additional Issue No. is answered accordingly. 
Additional Issue No. 2 - 


The charges proved are misconduct by way of habitual and unauthorized absenting from Workplace which is 
violation of Clause 29.5 of Standing Orders and is a major misconduct punishment for which includes 
termination also. 


It also comes out from the enquiry papers that, the Workman has been in the habit of committing the same 
type of misconduct and he was punished earlier also. Hence, keeping in view previous service records and the 
fact that he has been in the habit of committing the similar type of misconduct the punishment of dismissal is 
held to be proportionate to the charge. 


Additional Issue No.2 is answered accordingly. 
On the basis of above discussion the reference is answered as follows: 
AWARD 


Holding, the act of Management of Bhilai Steel Plant in dismissing service of Shri Dhani Ram, 
Ex-Sr. Operative Gr. 2, w.e.f 0..204 justified in law. His legal representatives are held entitled to no 
relief. 


No order as to cost.

l. The workman/claimant has filed the present claim petition under Section 33-A of the Industrial Disputes

sizeable number of workers in NFL Naya Nangal Unit. The complainant-union along with other two union 
espoused the genuine cause of the workers of NFL Naya Nangal Unit regarding illegal and arbitrary transfers of 
the workmen from the NFL Naya Nangal Unit to other units of the National Fertilizers Ltd. against the certified 
standing orders applicable to this NFL Naya Nangal Unit. Upon failure of the conciliation proceedings by the 
Assistant Labur Commissioner(C) Jalandhar, the report was sent to the Govt. of India, Ministry of Labour dated 
29.08.20i8 copy of which is attached as Annexure-A. the management in gross violation of the provisions of the 
ID Act 947, transferred the workman, Sr. Engineering Assistant(Mech)SG-III to Bhatinda and relieved him on 
25.0.20i8 copy of which is attached as Annexure-C. The management is in habit of flouting the provisions of the 
ID Act as in the same fashion the management transferred as many as six persons from this Naya Nangal Unit to 
different units when conciliation proceedings were pending before the Conciliation Officer, Jalandhar but no 
action was taken then by the conciliation officer against the management. The workman specifically given request 
which is attached as Annexure-D that he remains sick and aged 55 years and having lot of responsibilities towards 
his family at this advance age. In view of the above, it is therefore prayed that management may be summoned 
and the transfer of the workman may be stayed and the management of NFL Nangal Unit may be directed to allow 
the workman to join duty at NFL Nangal Unit and the workman may be compensated suitably. 


2. Management has not filed any written statement. 


3. On 27.0i.202I, both the parties are present before this Tribunal and the workman Prem Chand vide his 
separate statement stated that his grievances have been settled with the management and he is not pressing the 
present application and it may be dismissed. The workman has _ prayed to the Court that the complaint be decided 
in the light of his statement. 


4. It is now well settled position in law that any settlement arrived at between the parties is legally binding upon 
both the parties in terms of the provisions of Section 8 of the ID Act. In view of the amicable settlement, there is 
no requirement to proceed with the present application. Statement of the workman shall form the integral part of 
the order. File after completion be consigned in the record room. 


A.K. SINGH, Presiding Officer-cum Link Officer
